ClayQuant

Calculation of X-ray powder diffraction patterns of interstratified clay minerals, and quantification of clay mineral assemblages from oriented mounts
User and reference manual · Program version 0.1.0 · September 2026

Scope. ClayQuant computes one-dimensional (00l) and three-dimensional (hkl) X-ray powder diffraction patterns for mica-type (illite), chlorite and kaolinite layer structures, for the ethylene glycol–smectite complex, and for randomly or non-randomly interstratified two-component stacks of these layers, with arbitrary preferred orientation and crystallite thickness distribution. It then uses those calculated patterns to quantify the clay mineral assemblage of a clay separate measured as three oriented mounts (air-dried, ethylene glycol-solvated and heated), by non-negative least squares over the whole pattern.

The program is written in Python, is operated through a local browser interface or from the command line, and is distributed as source. This manual documents the physical model, the implementation, the operating procedure, every control of the interface, the output files, and the tests by which the program was verified.

1 Introduction

1.1 Purpose

Quantitative analysis of clay mineral assemblages by X-ray diffraction is made difficult by three properties of the minerals themselves. Clay minerals are platy, so a specimen prepared for analysis is strongly textured rather than randomly oriented. They are frequently interstratified, so that a crystallite is a stack of two or more different layer types and produces neither the pattern of one end member nor a superposition of both. And they are finely divided, so that crystallites are only a few tens of layers thick and their reflections are correspondingly broad. None of these is a defect of the measurement; all three are properties of the material that a calculation must reproduce before a quantification can mean anything.

ClayQuant addresses these by calculating the pattern that each candidate phase would produce under the conditions of the measurement — its texture, its crystallite thickness, its layer spacing, the instrument's emission profile and slit geometry — and then fitting the measured pattern as a non-negative combination of those calculated patterns.

1.2 What the program does and does not do

It does:

  • compute 00l and hkl intensities from crystal structures supplied as CIF;
  • compute the diffracted intensity of a two-component interstratified stack with arbitrary junction probabilities and a distribution of crystallite thicknesses;
  • apply preferred orientation, Lorentz–polarization, beam overflow, an arbitrary emission profile and an adjustable peak shape;
  • read the common vendor file formats, determine the 2θ zero error, model the background, identify kaolinite and expandable clay from the three-mount comparison, identify accompanying non-clay minerals, and fit and report the assemblage.

It does not:

  • refine structures. Cell parameters, atomic coordinates, site occupancies and displacement parameters are taken as given and are not adjusted against the data. ClayQuant is not a Rietveld program;
  • refine peak positions, widths or orientation continuously. The fit chooses among pre-computed patterns, so the achievable agreement is limited by how finely the library samples those parameters (§3.3, §9);
  • report weight percent. What is reported is each phase's share of diffracted intensity; the conversion requires a reference intensity ratio per phase (§2.13);
  • model three-component interstratifications, or interstratifications with a lateral (ab) component of disorder beyond that implied by the treatment of §2.12.

1.3 Notation and conventions

Throughout, λ is the wavelength in ångström, θ the Bragg angle, and

s = 2 sinθ / λ = 1/d (1.1)

the length of the scattering vector, in å−1. Note that s is defined here without the factor 2π and without the factor ½ used in some crystallographic literature; the quantity q = sinθ/λ = s/2 is used only as the argument of scattering factors and displacement factors, matching International Tables convention. The stacking axis of a layer structure is c*, and heights along it are given in ångström and denoted z. Layer repeat distances are denoted dA, dB. Intensities are per unit incident flux and are reported in arbitrary units, since only relative intensities enter the analysis.

1.4 Related programs

The one-dimensional part of the calculation follows the same physics as NEWMOD (Reynolds), PyXRD (Dumon & Van Ranst) and Sybilla, all of which implement the matrix formalism of §2.5. ClayQuant differs from these chiefly in coupling the calculation directly to a whole-pattern non-negative least-squares quantification, in computing the three-dimensional hkl contribution of the host phases from crystal structures rather than treating only basal reflections, and in being open source and scriptable.

2 Theory

2.1 The oriented mount

A clay separate is deposited on a glass slide so that the platelets lie with (001) close to the slide surface. In Bragg–Brentano reflection geometry the diffraction vector is always parallel to the specimen normal, so such a specimen presents predominantly its basal (00l) reflections. The degree to which this is true is a property of the preparation, not a constant, and is treated here as an adjustable texture parameter (§2.9).

Three mounts of the same separate are measured:

MountTreatmentDiagnostic role
Air-driedas deposited, equilibrated with laboratory airreference state
Glycol-solvatedexposed to ethylene glycol vapourexpandable layers swell to a two-layer complex near 16.9 å
Heatedtypically 500 °Ckaolinite dehydroxylates and its 7.15 å reflection is lost; chlorite survives

The quantitative fit is performed on the glycol-solvated mount, because glycolation separates the expandable from the non-expandable component and resolves the illite/smectite series, which in the air-dried state overlap near 10–14 å.

2.2 Scattering factors and the structure factor

Atomic scattering factors f0(q) are evaluated from the eleven-parameter analytical expansion of Waasmaier & Kirfel (1995),

f0(q) = c + Σi=15 ai exp(−bi q2) (2.1)

valid to q = 6 å−1, with q = sinθ/λ. Ionic species are used where the tabulation provides them and the CIF specifies a charge; otherwise the neutral atom is used, and a species that is not tabulated falls back to its neutral atom with a warning. Isotropic displacement is applied as

T(q) = exp(−B q2) (2.2)

with B in å2. Where a CIF reports Uiso, the conversion B = 8π2U is applied. The structure factor of a reflection hkl is then

F(hkl) = Σj nj fj(q) exp(−Bjq2) exp[2πi(hxj + kyj + lzj)] (2.3)

summed over the symmetry-expanded content of the unit cell, with nj the site occupancy. Symmetry operations are taken from the CIF as written, parsed into a rotation and a translation, applied to each asymmetric-unit site, and duplicate positions removed within a tolerance of 10−4 in fractional coordinates.

2.3 The one-dimensional layer model

For a basal reflection h = k = 0, equation (2.3) reduces to

F(00l) = Σj nj fj Tj exp(2πi l zj) (2.4)

which depends only on the fractional coordinate along c, whatever the cell angles: the scalar product of the reciprocal vector (00l) with a position xa+yb+zc is lz exactly. No projection correction is required. The basal spacing follows from the triclinic metric as

d(001) = 1/|c*| = V / (ab sinγ) (2.5)

A layer model is therefore a list of scatterers at absolute heights z (in ångström) within one layer of repeat distance d, each with an occupancy and a displacement parameter, together with the continuous layer structure factor

F(s) = Σj nj fj(s/2) exp(−Bj s2/4) exp(2πi s zj) (2.6)

Here s is continuous, not restricted to l/d: an interstratified stack is not periodic and scatters at every s, which is precisely what §2.5 integrates.

Deriving a layer model from a polytype cell

The structures available for illite, chlorite and kaolinite are multi-layer polytypes: illite ICSD 90144 is a two-layer C2/c cell, kaolinite 2M ICSD 30285 a two-layer C1c1 cell. Successive layers in these polytypes are related by operations of the form (x, −y, z+½) — a rotation or reflection in the ab plane combined with a translation of exactly half the cell along c. Such an operation leaves the projection of the electron density on c* unchanged. The projected density therefore repeats every d(001)/n, and a single-layer model is obtained exactly by folding all atomic heights modulo that distance. This is done automatically; the fold is exact for the 2M1 and IIb polytypes used here and was verified numerically (§A.1).

Consequence. Because only the projection on c* enters, kaolinite 1M and kaolinite 2M have nearly identical basal series and are not distinguishable from 00l intensities alone. They are separable only through their hkl reflections, which in a strongly oriented mount are weak. Both are provided, and a fit that divides intensity between them should not be read as a polytype determination.

2.4 Basal reflections of a periodic stack

For a crystallite of N identical layers of thickness d, the amplitudes add with a phase 2πs d per layer and

I(s) = |F(s)|2 · sin2(πN s d) / sin2(πs d) (2.7)

the familiar Laue interference function, which has maxima of height N2 at s = l/d and a width in s of about 1/(Nd). Equation (2.7) is the A = B limit of the general result below, and is used as a closed-form check on it (§A.1).

2.5 Interstratification: the matrix method

Consider a crystallite of N layers stacked along c*, each of type A or B, with layer structure factors FA(s), FB(s) and thicknesses dA, dB. Let the sequence be a stationary first-order Markov chain with transition matrix P, where Pmn is the probability that a layer of type m is followed by one of type n, and with stationary proportions W satisfying WP = W.

The scattered amplitude is

A(s) = Σj=1N Ftj(s) exp(2πi s zj),    zj = Σk<j dtk (2.8)

and the expected intensity ⟨|A|2⟩ separates into a self term and a pair term,

I(s) = Σj ⟨|Ftj|2⟩ + 2 Re Σj<k ⟨Ftk F*tj exp(2πi s(zk−zj))⟩ (2.9)

Define the matrix

Tmn(s) = Pmn exp(2πi s dm) (2.10)

Then the sum over all sequences of n steps from type m to type p, weighted by probability and carrying the accumulated phase, is exactly [Tn]mp. Writing fm = WmF*m, the pair at separation n contributes fTTnF, and counting the (N−n) pairs at that separation gives

I(s) = N Σm Wm|Fm|2 + 2 Re Σn=1N−1 (N−n) fTTnF (2.11)

which is the result implemented. Dividing by N and letting N→∞ gives the Kakinoki–Komura form

I∞(s)/N = Re{ fT[2(I−T)−1−I]F } (2.12)

since Σn≥1Tn = (I−T)−1−I and fTF = ΣWm|Fm|2. ClayQuant uses the finite form (2.11), because crystallite thickness controls basal peak width and the infinite limit would give delta functions.

On the phase convention. The distance from the origin of layer j to that of layer j+1 is the thickness of layer j, not of layer j+1. This is why the exponential in (2.10) carries dm, the thickness of the layer being left. Using the other convention transposes the roles of the two components and is a common source of error; the implementation is checked against the pure end members and against the closed form (2.7) for this reason (§A.1).

2.6 Crystallite thickness

Real specimens contain crystallites of many thicknesses. Averaging (2.11) over a distribution p(N) and normalising per layer gives

I(s)/⟨N⟩ = ΣmWm|Fm|2 + 2 Re Σn≥1 G(n) fTTnF (2.13)

with the pair weights

G(n) = ⟨max(N−n, 0)⟩ / ⟨N⟩ (2.14)

so the thickness distribution enters through one vector of weights, computed once and reused at every s. The distribution used is lognormal in N, parameterised by its mean ⟨N⟩ and by the width β of the underlying normal distribution in ln N, following the crystallite size distribution (CSDS) treatment standard in this field (Drits, Eberl & Środoń). G(n) is normalised so that G(0) = 1.

Crystallite thickness is the dominant control on basal peak width. For a 10 å layer, a mean of 10 layers gives a 001 width of order 0.8° 2θ, while a well-crystallised illite may show 0.12°, which requires of order 70 layers (§A.7). It cannot be assumed; it must either be spanned by the library or determined from the data.

2.7 Ordering and Reichweite

The transition matrix carries the ordering. For a two-component system with proportions WA, WB:

CaseTransition probabilitiesDescription
Random, R = 0PAB = WB, PBA = WA a layer's identity is independent of its neighbour
Ordered, R = 1PAB > WB unlike layers tend to alternate; the limit PAB = 1 at WA = ½ is a regular alternation (rectorite-like)
SegregatedPAB < WB like layers cluster; the limit PAB = 0 is a physical mixture

Ordering is expressed through a single parameter PAB, from which the remaining probabilities follow by the stationarity and normalisation conditions WAPAB = WBPBA and PmA+PmB = 1. Values of PAB for which any probability would fall outside [0,1] are rejected. The supplied reference library is computed for the random case, which is the appropriate default for illite/smectite and chlorite/smectite in most sedimentary settings; ordered stacks can be computed in the simulator or by calling the library builder directly.

2.8 The Lorentz–polarization factor

Which Lorentz factor applies to an oriented clay aggregate measured on a diffractometer is a genuine and long-standing question, and the choice matters: the two candidate conventions differ by a factor l across a basal series after normalisation at 001, so an incorrect choice distorts every relative basal intensity and therefore every quantification derived from them.

The two candidates are the random-powder (Debye–Scherrer) form

LPpowder = (1 + cos22θ) / (2 sin2θ cosθ) (2.15)

and the single-crystal form appropriate to a one-dimensionally periodic, perfectly oriented specimen,

LPcrystal = (1 + cos22θ) / (2 sin 2θ) (2.16)

Bradley (1954) and Schoen (1962) found the random-powder factor to work for oriented aggregates; MacEwan, Amil & Brown (1961) argued for something intermediate. The matter was settled empirically by Reynolds (1965), who showed for an ethylene glycol–montmorillonite complex (his Table 2) and independently for a dry Na-montmorillonite (his Table 4) that the random-powder factor is required to reproduce observed basal intensities, the single-crystal factor giving large deviations — for the dry montmorillonite, a calculated 003 intensity of 141 against an observed 55.

ClayQuant therefore uses (2.15) by default. This is not merely a convention: the published one-dimensional clay layer models, including the glycol–smectite model used here, were refined under it, and their structure factors are only consistent when it is applied. Equation (2.16) is selectable for comparison. A monochromator-modified polarization factor,

p = (1 + cos22θ cos22θM) / (1 + cos22θM) (2.17)

is available for a crystal-monochromated beam.

2.9 Preferred orientation

Texture is described by the March–Dollase model (March 1932; Dollase 1986). For a reflection whose scattering vector makes an angle α with the texture axis,

P(α; r) = (r2cos2α + sin2α/r)−3/2 (2.18)

The texture axis is c*, the platelet normal, which in Bragg–Brentano reflection geometry coincides with the specimen normal. r = 1 is a random powder; r < 1 describes platelets lying in the specimen plane, enhancing 00l and suppressing hk0. The function conserves total scattered intensity, its average over the sphere being unity, so r redistributes intensity rather than creating it.

Preferred orientation does not change a purely basal pattern. For every 00l reflection α = 0, so P = r−3 for all of them alike: a common scale factor. The March–Dollase parameter therefore has no effect on the shape of a basal series, and acts only on the ratio of basal to non-basal intensity. This is why the ten orientation parameters of the reference library change an interstratified pattern only through its hkl contribution (§2.12), and why r cannot be determined from basal reflections alone.

2.10 Beam overflow

The Lorentz factor diverges as 1/sin2θ, but a real measurement does not, because at low angle the irradiated length of a flat specimen,

Lirr(θ) = R γ / sinθ (2.19)

with R the goniometer radius and γ the equatorial divergence in radians, exceeds the specimen and part of the beam misses it. Only the intercepted fraction diffracts:

φ(θ) = min[1, Lspec sinθ / (R γ)] (2.20)

This matters precisely where clay basal reflections lie. Reynolds (1965) avoided the correction by changing beam slits with angle so that the beam never exceeded his specimen, following Klug & Alexander (1954); with the fixed slits of a modern instrument it must be applied, or every calculated pattern carries an unphysical low-angle ramp. The specimen length, goniometer radius and divergence are settable; for a variable-divergence (automatic) slit, which keeps the irradiated length constant, the correction should be disabled.

2.11 Emission profile and peak shape

The source is described as a sum of Lorentzian-weighted lines, each with its own wavelength, relative intensity and intrinsic width. The default Cu Kα profile is the five-line description

Lineλ (å)Relative weightWidth
11.5347530.01593.6854
21.5405960.56910.4370
31.5410580.07620.6000
41.5444100.25170.5200
51.5447210.08710.6200

Every reflection is generated once per emission line, at the 2θ corresponding to that line's wavelength and scaled by its weight, so the Kα1/Kα2 separation emerges naturally and correctly with angle rather than being imposed. Other profiles, including a single Kα1 line, are available.

The instrumental profile is a pseudo-Voigt whose Gaussian width follows the Caglioti relation

FWHM2 = U tan2θ + V tanθ + W (2.21)

with a mixing parameter η between Gaussian and Lorentzian, optionally combined with a Scherrer broadening from a finite in-plane crystallite dimension. Note that broadening along c* is not imposed through (2.21): for interstratified phases it arises physically from the crystallite thickness distribution of §2.6.

2.12 Assembling a pattern

A pattern of a discrete crystalline phase is computed by enumerating every reciprocal lattice point within the measurable range, evaluating (2.3), and applying preferred orientation, Lorentz–polarization and beam overflow before convolution with the emission profile and peak shape. Reflections are enumerated individually rather than by symmetry-equivalent family, so multiplicity is accounted for by the enumeration itself and each reflection receives its own March–Dollase factor according to its own angle to c* — which is what the texture correction requires.

An interstratified pattern is assembled from two contributions:

  1. the continuous basal intensity of §2.5, evaluated at every point of the 2θ grid and carrying LP, beam overflow and the emission profile;
  2. the non-basal (hkl, k≠0 or h≠0) reflections of the host phase, computed from its crystal structure and scaled by their March–Dollase factors.
Approximation. Contribution (2) treats the non-basal scattering of an interstratified crystal as that of its host layer type, scaled by the host's proportion. This is an approximation. In reality, turbostratic stacking produces two-dimensional hk bands with a characteristic sawtooth profile rather than sharp three-dimensional reflections, and the interstratified component contributes its own non-basal scattering. The approximation is acceptable for a strongly oriented mount, where non-basal intensity is heavily suppressed by the texture, and it degrades as r approaches 1. The relative scaling of the two contributions is fixed by computing, for a pure host stack, the ratio of its basal intensity in the two formulations, so that a pure end member reproduces its own three-dimensional calculation (§A.1).

2.13 Quantification

The measured pattern y(2θ), after zero-error correction and background subtraction, is fitted as

y(2θ) ≈ Σp cp yp(2θ),    cp ≥ 0 (2.22)

over the library patterns yp, by non-negative least squares. The non-negativity constraint is physical — a phase cannot be present in negative amount — and has the useful side effect of producing a sparse solution, so that of several hundred candidate patterns only a handful take non-zero coefficients.

The solve is weighted. The variance of a counting measurement at a point is the number of counts recorded there, so the weight is

wi = 1 / max(yraw,i, 1) (2.23)

taken from the raw counts, before background subtraction: subtracting a background does not reduce the Poisson variance of the measurement. Weighting instead by the background-subtracted intensity — an easy error — places the greatest weight on the flat regions between peaks, where the subtracted value is near zero and only noise remains, and almost none on the peaks that carry the information (§A.9). Agreement is reported as

Rwp = [ Σwi (yi−ycalc,i)2 / Σwiyi2 ]1/2,    Rp = Σ|yi−ycalc,i| / Σ|yi| (2.24)

From coefficients to proportions

Two measures are reported for each phase, and they answer different questions:

Scattering share
the phase's fraction of the total calculated integrated intensity, cp∫yp / Σcq∫yq. This is the quantity the diffractogram actually measures.
Amplitude share
the phase's fraction of the summed scale factors, cp/Σcq. Broad interstratified patterns carry far more integrated area per unit peak height than a sharp discrete phase, so the two can differ by a factor of several.

A parameter the library stopped rather than determined

The fit chooses among pre-computed patterns (§3.3), so it cannot return a value the library does not hold. When a phase's coefficients collect on the lowest or highest value of a spanned parameter, the honest reading is not that the parameter equals that value but that the data wanted to go further and ran out of library: the answer is a bound, not a measurement. In a table of numbers that all look alike that difference is invisible, and it is the same signal that marks a refined parameter sitting on its limit — worth distrusting wherever it appears.

So every fit reports it. parameters_at_an_edge lists each phase and parameter whose fitted weight piles up on an end of its range, and the fit records the list in its metadata without being asked. Merely including an end value among others is not flagged; the default threshold is 80 % of a phase's coefficient.

Two cases look identical in a table of numbers and are not the same thing, so they are worded differently. A crystallite thickness sitting on the largest value calculated means the data wanted a larger one and the library should be extended. A composition sitting on 1.00 means the data wants the pure phase, and there is nothing beyond it to extend to — the fit has answered rather than run out of room, and the same goes for an orientation parameter at r = 1, which is a random powder. Advice to span those further is advice that cannot be taken, and a warning a user learns to ignore is worse than none.

What prompted it: a measured pure illite standard put 94 % of its illite on the 0.99 entry of the illite/smectite series, the highest the series went. That reported 1 % of smectite the specimen did not have, and reported the end of a range as though it were a composition. The series now reaches 1.00 (§3.3), and the chlorite/smectite series with it.

How much of an interstratified phase is the host

The library spans illite/smectite from 0.20 to 0.99 illite layers and groups every one of those entries under the phase name I/S. The name alone is therefore misleading at the ends of the series: a fit that settles on the 0.99/0.01 entry has found a stack of essentially pure illite, and a table reporting that as “I/S, 63 % of the pattern” reads as though 63 % of the specimen were an expandable clay. On a measurement of a pure illite standard that is the difference between accepting the material and rejecting it.

So each phase also reports the host-layer fraction the fit chose, averaged over its entries and weighted by their coefficients, with the expandable fraction as its complement. A discrete mineral reports 1. Read the two together: I/S at 0.99 is an illite, at 0.60 it is genuinely interstratified.

Weight percent

A third quantity is reported, and it is a weight percent. It needs no reference intensity ratios, because the calculated patterns carry the mass of what they were calculated from. A stored pattern is the calculated one divided by a normalisation se; the calculated one is for a single unit of the phase — one unit cell for a discrete mineral, one layer for an interstratified stack — of mass Me. So a fitted coefficient ce counts units, and

Wp ∝ kp Σe∈p ce Me / se (2.25)

with the constant of proportionality the same for every phase — it is the instrument, the irradiated volume and the counting time, which the phases of one measurement share — so the ratios are ratios of mass. This is the relation Rietveld analysis writes as W ∝ S(ZMV), in the form ClayQuant's normalisation calls for. Tested by building a specimen from known masses of library patterns and asking for the masses back, it returns them exactly (§A.14).

kp is 1, and that is the whole difficulty. Equation (2.25) assumes the calculated pattern accounts for everything the phase contributes. In an oriented mount it does not, because texture differs between minerals and between preparations, and the fit cannot tell a well-oriented phase from an abundant one. The effect is not a correction of a few percent. A basal series is multiplied by r−3 (§2.9), so a clay fitted at r = 0.13 is calculated to scatter 455 times more per gram than the same clay at r = 1, and the mass inferred for it falls by the same factor, while quartz — which does not plate onto the slide and is fitted at r = 1 — takes the mass the clays lose. Until kp has been measured for a preparation, read the weight percent as indicative and the clay-to-non-clay split as the least reliable part of it. The fitted r is reported beside every phase so this is visible rather than hidden.

Measuring kp. It is one factor per phase, covering texture, microabsorption and any error in the structural model together. To determine it, analyse specimens whose composition is known independently, through the same preparation routine, and solve for the factors that reproduce that composition — Calibration.from_known_composition does the arithmetic, and the factors are stored in a JSON file that the analysis loads. One way to obtain the known composition is to measure the same separate twice: once as a random mount spiked with an internal standard, which gives absolute weight fractions by the usual internal-standard method and is unaffected by texture because there is none; and once as the oriented mounts. The random mount fixes the composition, the oriented fit then yields kp. An oriented mount cannot be spiked usefully, since the standard does not orient as the clays do and its share in the mount is not its share in the suspension.

The other route needs no mixture at all: mount one pure mineral, and measure a standard of known weight separately through the same optics. Then the mass the specimen holds is known independently of any fit, and kp is what stands between it and the mass (2.25) infers. That is the external-standard method below, and §A.18 reports it.

The older route is still available for a laboratory that has measured reference intensity ratios of its own: Quantification.weight_percent divides each phase's share of diffracted intensity by its ratio.

An internal standard, and what the fit does not account for

Every weight percent above is a share of what was fitted, and sums to 100 however much of the specimen was left out. A mount holding amorphous material, or a mineral the library does not have, therefore reports every phase in it overstated by one common factor, and nothing inside the fit reveals the factor: the residual of a whole-pattern fit is not a measure of missing crystalline matter, because a missing phase's intensity is taken up by whatever else lies under it.

A weighed addition of a standard reveals it. If a mass fraction Wstd of a standard is mixed into the specimen before mounting, and the fit returns W′std for it on the relative basis, then every phase's weight percent of the specimen is

Wp = W′p · Wstd / W′std (2.26)

and what is left over, 100 − ΣpWp, is the amorphous content together with any crystalline phase absent from the fit. The measurement separates that sum from the phases that were fitted, but not into its two parts.

Pass the standard and its weight to the analysis (quantify(..., internal_standard=("Corundum", 20.0))) and the table gains an absolute column beside the relative one, with the unaccounted fraction reported alongside. A standard that was weighed in but does not appear in the fit leaves the analysis relative and says so, rather than scaling by a number it does not have. The absolute column is given on the whole-specimen basis only: a clay-mineral table is renormalised to 100 % by definition, so scaling it would mean nothing.

An internal standard belongs in a random mount, not an oriented one. The standard must share the specimen's texture for (2.26) to hold, and a spike added to a clay suspension does not: it does not plate onto the slide as the clays do, so its share of the mount is not its share of the suspension. Equation (2.26) is for a pressed random powder. This is also why the internal-standard route cannot by itself measure kp for an oriented mount (§A.15); an external standard can, and is treated next.

An external standard, and the absolute scale

The restriction just stated — that a standard mixed into an oriented mount cannot work — does not apply to a standard that is never mixed in. Measure a standard of known weight fraction on its own, under the same optics, and it is never asked to share the specimen's texture. That is the external-standard method of O'Connor and Raven (1988), and it is what turns the proportionality of (2.25) into an equality.

The standard's own measurement fixes one instrument constant,

K = Sstd(ZMV)std · (μ/ρ)std / Wstd (2.27)

and any later measurement on the same instrument then gives an absolute weight fraction without a spike,

Wp = Sp(ZMV)p · (μ/ρ)spec / K (2.28)

where S(ZMV) is, in ClayQuant's normalisation, exactly the sum ΣceMe/se of (2.25), and μ/ρ is the mass attenuation coefficient of the whole specimen at the wavelength used. Absorption enters because the two measurements sample different depths: a weakly absorbing specimen returns intensity from further down, and the ratio of the two coefficients corrects for it. absorption.py computes μ/ρ for a structure from its mass fractions and tabulated elemental coefficients at Cu Kα, and refuses — rather than guessing — for an element it does not hold.

Two conditions have to hold, and both are checkable rather than assumed. The specimen must be thicker than the beam penetrates, since (2.28) is derived for infinite thickness; penetration_depth and thick_enough give the depth sinθ/2μ and test a film against it, which for a clay mount matters most at low angle where the depth is smallest. And the two measurements must be made through the same optics: a difference in divergence slit, mask, counting time or tube setting changes K and is not recoverable afterwards. So ExternalStandard records the conditions of the standard's measurement and comparable_with names every difference it finds against a later one, rather than scaling by a constant that no longer applies.

For a mount of a known phase this reads backwards and measures kp directly: Wp is known, so calibration_factor returns the ratio of the mass (2.25) infers to the mass the specimen holds. That is the one route to kp for an oriented mount that does not need an independent analysis of a mixture, and §A.18 carries it out on four pure clay mounts against a corundum measured through the same optics.

Results are given on two bases: over all fitted phases, and over the clay minerals alone, renormalised to 100 % with the accompanying minerals removed. The latter is the customary basis for reporting a clay mineral assemblage.

3.3 The reference library

Because the fit selects among pre-computed patterns rather than refining parameters, the library must span the parameters that actually vary between specimens. Three are spanned:

DimensionValuesWhy it must be spanned
Preferred orientation r0.1 to 1.0 in steps of 0.1 texture is a property of the preparation, not of the mineral; it sets the ratio of basal to non-basal intensity
Mean crystallite thickness ⟨N⟩5, 15, 50 layers sets basal peak width; 10 layers give a 001 width near 0.8° where a well-crystallised illite shows 0.12°
Layer spacing dillite 9.95, 10.02, 10.10 å; chlorite 14.20, 14.35 å illite d(001) varies with interlayer potassium and hydration; an error of 0.07 å displaces the 001 by half a peak width

Together with the compositional series this gives, with default settings, 1751 patterns:

PhasePatternsComposition range
Illite/smectite (I/S)1440 16 compositions, 0.20/0.80 to 1.00/0.00
Chlorite/smectite (C/S)240 1.00/0.00, 0.95/0.05, 0.90/0.10, 0.85/0.15
Illite30discrete
Chlorite20discrete
Kaolinite 1M, 2M10 + 10discrete
Glycol–smectite1pure end member
Both series reach their pure end member, and that matters more than it looks. Without it the closest a pure illite could be described as was 0.99/0.01, and a fit of one piles its whole coefficient onto that entry: it reports 1 % of smectite the specimen does not have, and it reports the end of a range as though it were a composition (§2.13). A measured pure illite standard is what showed this, putting 94 % of its illite on the 0.99 entry. The end member is also not redundant with the discrete illite entries: those are three-dimensional powder patterns whose basal widths come from the instrumental profile, while the interstratified entries carry the crystallite thickness distribution of §2.6, which is what actually sets a basal width. Only through this series can a pure illite be fitted with its thickness spanned.

Each pattern is stored normalised to unit maximum above 4° 2θ, not to its global maximum. Intensity rises steeply towards zero angle — the Lorentz factor still diverges after the beam-overflow correction — and no clay basal reflection of interest lies below about 4°; normalising on that rise would shrink the diffraction peaks themselves and leave the fit poorly conditioned.

Each pattern also has its own smooth continuum stripped before storage. An interstratified stack of finite thickness scatters a genuine diffuse continuum rising towards zero angle, but in a measurement that continuum is inseparable from air scatter and the direct beam and is always treated as background. Leaving it in the basis patterns would let a phase absorb the measured background and inflate its apparent share.

For that reason every pattern is calculated over a wider range than it is stored on: one stripping window beyond each end, trimmed away afterwards. Peak stripping needs data on both sides of a point, so its estimate is unreliable within one window of either end (§A.11), and for a calculated clay pattern that is exactly where the diffuse continuum is largest. Moving the ends outside the stored range takes the continuum left standing at 3.5° on an I/S 0.80/0.20 pattern from 21 % of its strongest peak down to 5 %, with the peaks themselves unchanged. The lower limit of the calculation is 1° 2θ, below which the Lorentz factor is of no use.

3.4 Numerical notes

  • Symmetry operations are parsed by an explicit tokeniser, never by evaluating file content as code.
  • The matrix sum (2.13) is truncated at the largest N carrying appreciable weight; the 2×2 matrix powers are accumulated once for all grid points simultaneously.
  • Reflection enumeration is bounded by the measurable dmin at the longest wavelength in the emission profile.
  • The NNLS solve is that of Lawson & Hanson as implemented in SciPy, applied to the row-weighted system; with 1600 columns and about 1800 points a fit takes well under a second.

4 Installation and structure data

4.1 Installation

Requirements

ComponentRequirementNotes
Python3.10 or laterdeveloped and tested on 3.11
NumPy≥ 1.24required
SciPy≥ 1.10required, for the NNLS solver
Dash≥ 2.14extra gui; needed only for the interface
Plotly≥ 5.18extra gui; also used by the figure export
gemmi≥ 0.6extra import; needed only to import a TOPAS structure library
pytest≥ 7.4extra dev; needed only to run the test suite
Operating systemanypure Python; no compiler required. Linux, macOS and Windows
Disk~200 MBdependencies, plus 30–60 MB per stored reference library
Memory~1 GBa default library holds 1601 patterns on the measurement grid
Browserany currentthe interface runs locally at 127.0.0.1; nothing is sent over the network

Procedure

The supplied installer does the whole of this and checks the result. From the project directory:

# Linux, macOS, WSL
./install.sh

# Windows, in PowerShell
.\install.cmd
On Windows, start with install.cmd and not install.ps1. Every client installation of Windows ships with PowerShell script execution disabled, so running the PowerShell installer directly fails before it executes a line: 
.\install.ps1 : File ...\install.ps1 cannot be loaded because running
scripts is disabled on this system.

That is the machine's default and says nothing about the script. A .cmd file is not subject to the policy, so install.cmd starts PowerShell with the policy bypassed for that one invocation, passes its arguments through unchanged, and changes no setting on the computer. It can be double-clicked, and waits for a keypress before it closes, so an error can be read — set CLAYQUANT_NO_PAUSE to skip that. The equivalent typed by hand is

powershell -ExecutionPolicy Bypass -File .\install.ps1

Keep the .\: PowerShell does not run a program from the current directory unless told to, so a plain install.cmd is answered with “the term ‘install.cmd’ is not recognized”, which is about the path and not the file. cmd.exe does not mind either way. The same applies to running the program: use .\clayquant.cmd gui rather than .\clayquant.ps1 gui. The desktop and Start-menu shortcuts are unaffected, because they point at the environment's own clayquant-gui.exe rather than at a script.

The alternative, if a permanent change is preferred, is to allow local scripts for your own account once — no administrator rights needed:

Set-ExecutionPolicy -Scope CurrentUser -ExecutionPolicy RemoteSigned

A checkout made with git clone then runs as it stands. Files extracted from a downloaded ZIP carry Windows' mark-of-the-web and count as remote, so RemoteSigned still refuses them until the mark is removed with Unblock-File .\install.ps1. Cloning avoids the question altogether.

It selects an interpreter, builds the virtual environment, installs ClayQuant with its dependencies, verifies that the package imports, checks that every command it declares has been created and answers, and reports which clay structures it can find. Re-running it is safe: an environment of the right version is reused, one of the wrong version is rebuilt. Useful options are -y to answer prompts automatically, --python /path/to/python3.12 to force an interpreter, and --no-dev to omit the test and import extras.

Starting it from an icon

At the end of the installation you are asked whether to create a desktop icon and a menu entry. Answering yes writes what the desktop in question expects — a .desktop file on Linux, an application bundle in ~/Applications on macOS, a shortcut on the desktop and in the Start menu on Windows — pointing at the interpreter of the environment ClayQuant was installed in, so nothing has to be activated or on PATH. Double-clicking it starts the program and opens it in the default browser.

It can be done or undone at any time, and does not need the installer:

./clayquant shortcut            # create them
./clayquant shortcut --where    # say where they would go
./clayquant shortcut --remove   # take them away

For the icon, put an image called clayquant into assets/ and run the command again. Any common raster format will do and the spelling of the name does not matter — ClayQuant.PNG is found as readily as clayquant.png, which on a case-sensitive filesystem it otherwise would not be — and it is converted to the format each platform needs (.ico on Windows, .icns on macOS). The placeholder that ships with ClayQuant is called clayquant-placeholder.png so that a supplied icon always takes precedence over it and is never overwritten by an update. The command prints which file it used.

Run it again after every update. The commands (clayquant-gui and the rest) are written into the environment when the package is installed and at no other time, so an environment built from one version keeps that version's set of commands. Updating the source with git pull does not add a command the new version introduced, and it is then reported as not found although its code is in the checkout. Re-running the installer writes them all; §7 gives the module form to use meanwhile.
Why an installer rather than three commands. python -m venv runs whichever interpreter the name python resolves to, and each Python version carries its own venv module and ensurepip, with its own bundled wheels. On Ubuntu and WSL, python and python3 are frequently an older version than the one that was installed later, so the command fails with 
The virtual environment was not created successfully because ensurepip is
not available. ... apt install python3.10-venv

even on a machine where python3.12-venv is installed. Nothing is failing to "see" the newer Python: version 3.10 was invoked, and 3.10's package is the one missing. The immediate fix is to name the interpreter — python3.12 -m venv .venv — and the installer does this automatically, trying every interpreter it can find, newest first, testing each by actually building a throwaway environment, and naming the exact distribution package if none succeeds.

Doing it by hand

1. Obtain the source and create an isolated environment. Name the interpreter explicitly rather than relying on python.

git clone https://github.com/lomalaspina/ClayQuant.git
cd ClayQuant
python3.12 -m venv .venv          # or whichever version 3.10+ you have

2. Activate the environment.

# Linux and macOS
source .venv/bin/activate

# Windows, PowerShell
.venv\Scripts\Activate.ps1

# Windows, cmd.exe
.venv\Scripts\activate.bat

The PowerShell form is refused on a machine that has not had its execution policy changed, for the reason given under the procedure above; activate.bat from cmd.exe is never affected, and neither is clayquant.cmd, which needs no activation at all.

3. Install. The extras select optional components; installing all of them is normal for interactive use.

pip install -e ".[gui,import,dev]"

The editable install (-e) means edits to the source take effect without reinstalling. To install only what is needed to compute patterns from a script, omit the extras: pip install -e .

4. Verify the installation. The test suite takes about a minute.

pytest -q

Tests that need structure data are skipped automatically when it is absent, and report as s rather than as failures; see §4.2. With no structure data installed, expect 29 passed and 10 skipped; with the four CIFs in place, 45 passed. Any failure indicates a problem and should be reported.

5. Provide structure data (§4.2), build a reference library (§4.4), and start the interface:

clayquant-gui

which prints a local address, by default http://127.0.0.1:8050, to open in a browser. Use --port to choose another port and --host to bind an interface other than the loopback.

Upgrading. After pulling a new revision, re-run pip install -e ".[gui,import,dev]" to pick up any dependency change, and rebuild the reference library if the pattern calculation has changed. Stored libraries carry the metadata of the settings they were built with, and a library built by an older revision is read but may not correspond to the current calculation.

4.2 Structure data and licensing

No structure data is distributed with ClayQuant. The crystal structures it uses are ICSD entries, which are licensed by FIZ Karlsruhe and may not be redistributed. They must be exported from your own subscription. The repository's ignore rules are written so that a local copy cannot be committed by accident.

Export each of the following as CIF and put it in the structure directory. The name given is the one ClayQuant looks for first, but it is not required: a file is also accepted if its name carries the ICSD code, or the phase name with its polytype. Kaolinite_1M_63192.cif and Illite_ICSD_90144.cif are both found, in any letter case.

PhaseICSDFile nameStructure reference
Illite90144illite_ICSD_90144.cif Gualtieri (2000)
Chlorite (clinochlore IIb-4)164234chlorite_ICSD_164234.cif Zanazzi, Comodi, Nazzareni & Andreozzi (2009)
Kaolinite 1M63192kaolinite_1M_ICSD_63192.cif Bish & Von Dreele (1989)
Kaolinite 2M30285kaolinite_2M_ICSD_30285.cif Gruner (1932)

These directories are searched, in this order, and all of them are searched rather than only the first that exists — the program is as likely to be started from the home directory as from the project, and a file that is plainly there should not be reported missing over where the shell happened to be:

  1. the path in the environment variable CLAYQUANT_STRUCTURE_DIR, if set;
  2. a structures folder in the current working directory;
  3. the current working directory itself;
  4. the structures folder of a source checkout;
  5. the package data directory.

To see what was looked for, where, and what was found:

python -c "from clayquant.models import describe_structure_search as d; print(d())"

The same report is printed when a structure cannot be loaded, so an error names the directories that were searched rather than one expected file name.

The glycol–smectite layer requires no file. It is the published one-dimensional model of Reynolds (1965), transcribed into the source with its provenance, and is reproduced under §A.2.

4.3 Importing a TOPAS structure library

This step and the next have a window each, which can be double-clicked. Both were command lines with paths in them, and typing a Windows path into a terminal is where this program lost people. clayquant shortcut now puts three icons on the desktop and in the menu — the interface, Import structures and Build library — and each of the latter two opens a small window with file pickers, a Run button and the log of what happened. The same windows open from a checkout with .\clayquant.cmd setup import-structures and .\clayquant.cmd setup build-library (./clayquant on Linux and macOS). The command lines described below are unchanged and remain the scriptable route.

The work runs in a worker thread and the window polls it, because building a library takes minutes and a window that stops repainting for minutes is a window people force-quit. Anything the job prints — including the import's report of phases that do not match the mass TOPAS states for them — appears in the window rather than on a console a double-clicked program does not have. The icons run python -m clayquant.tools rather than a console script, because the scripts are written into the environment at install time and at no other, so an icon naming one would break for anybody who pulled a version that added it without reinstalling (§4.1).

The accompanying non-clay minerals — quartz, feldspars, carbonates, sulphates, oxides — come from a structure library of your own. ClayQuant reads the jEdit macro-menu form in which TOPAS structure collections are commonly distributed: an XML file whose items each insert a TOPAS str block with a phase name, cell parameters, space group and site lines.

clayquant-import-structures my_structures.xml -o structures/phases.json

Space group symbols are expanded to explicit symmetry operations with gemmi, including the origin-choice settings that TOPAS writes as a trailing letter (Fd-3mS for origin choice 1, Fd-3mZ for choice 2; see §A.3). The operations are stored in the generated database, so gemmi is not needed afterwards.

The generated database is derived from licensed structure data and is likewise kept out of version control.

Structures from one of your own refinements

TOPAS writes a refinement's result back in the syntax it read, so a refinement's .out — or its .inp — is itself a structure library, of the few phases that refinement contained. The same command reads it, and decides which kind of file it has by looking:

clayquant-import-structures M_26_1041_air.out -o structures/refined.json

Several sources may be given, in increasing order of authority: where two name the same phase the later one is kept, so a refinement laid over a library keeps the library's breadth and takes the refinement's structure for the phases it covers.

clayquant-import-structures my_structures.xml M_26_1041_air.out -o structures/phases.json

For the clay minerals the refined structure goes further than the phase database: it can replace the published CIF the pattern library is calculated from.

clayquant-build-library --refined-structures M_26_1041_air.out

Which phases to take is chosen per mineral, with --refined-only or --refined-except, because the judgement differs between them. Keeping a published structure that can be cited, while taking the refined ones that describe the specimen better, is a reasonable decision rather than a missed opportunity:

clayquant-build-library --refined-structures M_26_1041_air.out --refined-except chlorite

This is worth doing, and worth doing for the clays in particular, because the octahedral Fe-for-Mg and Fe-for-Al substitutions are refinable against the basal intensities, differ from one deposit to the next, and change those intensities substantially — iron scatters about twice as strongly as the magnesium it replaces. On the specimen of §A.16 it improves Rwp from 35.9 % to 31.2 %, and the occupancies rather than the refined cells account for nearly all of that.

Do not extend it to the accompanying minerals without checking. Measured on the same specimen, taking their refined cells as well costs 3 points of Rwp (§A.16). Part of the reason is identifiable — quartz is also the zero-error standard (§5.3), so replacing its structure puts the calibration and the fitted cell out of step — and part is not. Where a library structure is wrong rather than merely someone else's, overriding it is still right: a refinement is how the incomplete cordierite of §A.14 was found to be incomplete, and supplies the sites it is missing.

A refinement that models its clays as hkl_Is peak sets, which is the usual way to refine an oriented mount, contains no clay structure at all; the import says so rather than reporting success with nothing in it. A refinement also covers only the phases it contained: one that fits kaolinite as the 2M polytype supplies no 1M, and the CIF for that is still wanted. The refined structures replace the CIFs one phase at a time; they do not remove the need for the folder.

Or as a CIF in the structure folder

The refined structures do not pass through the structure folder at all — the CIF files there are untouched, and the substitution happens when the pattern library is calculated. There is a second route, though, and it is the one most people will reach for first: put a CIF carrying the refined values into the folder like any other. It works, and TOPAS will have written the file already if the refinement carried Out_CIF_STR(...) for the phase.

Two details of such a file are handled, because both would otherwise cost the user the change they were trying to make. TOPAS writes a mineral name as ?Clinochlore?, using ? where CIF wants a quote, and the marks are stripped rather than kept as part of the name. And the file arrives named after the phase as the refinement called it, so a chlorite refined as Clinochlore arrives as Clinochlore.cif, which carries neither the ICSD code nor the key chlorite; the mineral's other names are now consulted, where before such a file matched nothing, the published structure was used instead, and nothing said so.

Which route to use is not a matter of taste. The structure folder is global: one file serves every specimen analysed afterwards. A refined occupancy belongs to one specimen — the iron content of a chlorite is a property of the deposit, and two specimens from different formations refine to octahedral compositions that are not close to each other. Put one specimen's refined chlorite in the folder and every later sample is calculated with that specimen's iron content, which is a harder mistake to notice than a missing file. --refined-structures keeps the coupling visible and per-analysis: the library is built from the refinement of the specimen it is going to be used on. Reach for the folder only for a structure meant as a better generic default than the published one — a composition typical of the material a laboratory usually sees — and name it so it says which.

What it reads, and what it reports

A structure library kept in a laboratory is written partly by hand and partly by TOPAS, and the two differ. The import reads both: a value carrying the backtick TOPAS puts on a refined parameter (16.875164`, or with a limit welded on as 9.663417`_LIMIT_MIN_9.5); an occupancy given as an expression with the value TOPAS last evaluated after a colon (occ Fe+2 =FeMgOCC;:0.99996`), which keeps a split site split instead of putting a full atom on each half; a space group written with spaces ("C c c m"); a comment after str; and a second structure block that takes its cell from the first by name (a =a_Calcite;), which is how a two-component phase for a crystallinity distribution is written.

Anything not imported is named. A phase that cannot be read is listed with the reason — no cell, no space group, no sites — and a phase that lists reflections rather than atoms (hkl_Is, a Pawley or amorphous entry) is named as such, since ClayQuant calculates from structures and has nothing to calculate from. Items that are headings or helper macros are passed over silently, as a menu is full of them. Before this, an item that could not be read was dropped before it became a record, so it was absent from every count afterwards: adding a phase to the library and re-importing gave the same number of phases as before, with nothing to say why.

4.4 Building the reference library

A library is built once for a given instrument configuration and measurement grid, and reused. Build it on the same 2θ grid as the measurements.

clayquant-build-library -o library/clays.npz

Building the default library takes about three minutes. Within the interface the same operation is available as Build library now, using the current instrument settings.

Chlorite compositions

The library holds one chlorite by default, the published structure, and that is the recommended setting. The two octahedral sheets of a chlorite take iron for magnesium in proportions that vary from one deposit to the next, iron scatters about twice as strongly as the magnesium it replaces, and each sheet sits at a definite height in the layer, so the composition does act directly on the basal intensities a quantification is read from. Whether that matters enough to fit is a separate question, and on the two pure chlorites of §A.17 it did not: the fit improved the residual only 1.5 to 1.7 times, drove one specimen to implausibly little iron, and ran against the bound of the crystallite-thickness grid.

So the facility is there for a specimen where the evidence calls for it, and is off by default. Unlike the illite/smectite ratio there is no generic set of compositions worth spanning; fit the composition to a measured pattern of a pure chlorite, check that the residual improves by enough to be worth having and that nothing lands on a bound, and only then calculate the library for the values that came out:

clayquant-build-library --chlorite-iron 0.35/0.20,0.55/0.30

Each pair is the iron occupancy of the 2:1 layer's octahedral sheet and of the interlayer hydroxide sheet. Every pair gets its own set of chlorite patterns, all grouped under the phase chlorite, so the fit chooses among compositions as it already chooses among layer spacings and orientations, and the quantification reports one chlorite. The cell mass follows the substitution, so the weight percent is consistent with whichever composition the fit chooses.

To measure the pairs, from a pattern of the pure mineral:

from clayquant.composition import fit_chlorite_iron
from clayquant.io import read_pattern

fit = fit_chlorite_iron(read_pattern("Chlorite_pure.xrdml"), instrument)
print(fit.describe())

The fit uses ratios of basal intensities within the one pattern, not the intensities themselves, so it needs neither a standard nor a known amount of material nor a known texture: preferred orientation multiplies a basal series by a single factor and divides straight out. It reports the residual beside the residual of the published structure, so a composition that is no improvement says so — and reports the crystallite thickness it settled on, because one at the edge of the grid means the composition absorbed something that was not composition.

Check the integration window before believing the result. A clay basal reflection has a diffuse tail from stacking disorder that carries much of its area, so a window that looks ample beside the peak width can hold a different fraction of each order — which is exactly what a ratio of orders responds to. §A.17 records a conclusion drawn from a window too narrow by a factor of three, and its retraction.

4.5 A library from measured peak lists

Everything above calculates a pattern from atomic positions. This is the other case: a reference pattern built from a table of d-spacings and relative intensities, which is the form a powder diffraction file entry takes. It is an addition — the clay library is still built from structures by §4.4, and a peak-list library is a separate file built separately.

What it cannot do, and why the clays are not in it. ICDD's PDF-2 — the set a local HighScore installation usually searches, whose entry numbers look like 00-012-0219 — holds per entry a table of interplanar spacings, relative intensities and often the diffraction indices. It holds no atomic coordinates; those are in PDF-4+. So an entry from it can give a pattern and cannot give a structure, and two things follow that no amount of work will change.

An illite/smectite pattern is not a sum of reflections at all. It comes from the matrix method (§2.5), which needs the layer structure factor as a continuous function of the scattering vector, and that needs scatterers at heights within the layer. A table of spacings cannot supply it, so an interstratified phase cannot be built from a file entry — only a discrete one, which is the opposite of the point. And a weight percent needs the mass of what the pattern was calculated from (§2.13); a peak list was not calculated from anything with a mass, so a peak-list phase has no weight percent of its own. That is why it is a separate file: mixing the two kinds behind one interface would make the weight percent quietly wrong for some of them.

Where it earns its place is the accompanying minerals. Quartz, the feldspars and calcite enter the fit as discrete phases, and a file entry's intensities are measured, on a real specimen with its real substitutions — which a calculated pattern from one published structure need not match any better. So a peak-list library is a reasonable thing to fit those against, and to compare against the calculated ones.

One correction is applied and it is not cosmetic. An entry's intensities are observed, so they already carry the Lorentz–polarization factor at the angle each line was measured at, while the pattern assembler applies that factor itself. Passing them through unchanged would apply it twice — a factor of thirty across a 4–40° scan, tilting the pattern end to end. The observed intensity is therefore divided by the factor on the way in and the assembler puts it back, so the pattern reproduces the entry at the entry's own geometry and still responds correctly to a change of instrument description. Tested by integrating each peak of the result and comparing with the entry, which agrees to 0.5 %.

Preferred orientation needs the indices and the cell, because the March–Dollase factor is a function of the angle between a reflection and c*. An entry carrying both can be spanned over r as the clay library is; an entry without them raises rather than guessing, since treating unindexed reflections as basal would enhance every line in the entry alike, which is not what an oriented mount does to anything. Such an entry contributes one pattern at r = 1, and the library records which entries those were.

The input

One block per phase, in a plain text file, which is what a powder diffraction file entry can be copied into:

PHASE   Montmorillonite-18A
SOURCE  ICDD PDF 00-012-0219
CELL    5.17 8.94 15.0 90 90 90
#   d(A)     I    h  k  l
  15.000   100    0  0  1
   4.490    80    1  1  0
   2.570    60

PHASE starts a block and is the only required line. SOURCE is free text, carried into the pattern's metadata so a fit can be traced back to the entry it came from. CELL takes the six cell parameters and is needed only for orientation. Then two or more columns: the spacing in ångström, the relative intensity, and optionally the indices, either as three columns or as one token such as 001. A line that looks like data and cannot be read raises with its number — a peak list silently one row short is a pattern wrong in a way nothing downstream can notice.

A powder diffraction file is licensed data. A library built from one is a derived work of it and belongs with your own files — not in a repository and not in anything shared, which is the same position the ICSD structures are in (§4.2). Nothing of the kind ships with ClayQuant: the input is supplied by whoever holds the licence. Entries can be quoted in a report by their file number, which is what the number is for.

5 Operating procedure

5.1 Specimen preparation assumed

ClayQuant assumes the preparation customary for clay mineral analysis: the bulk sample is ground, the clay fraction separated by sedimentation or centrifugation, and the separate deposited on glass slides to give oriented mounts, of which one is left air-dried, one solvated with ethylene glycol and one heated, typically to 500 °C. A bulk (randomly oriented) measurement of the whole sample is useful context but is not required by the program.

5.2 Step 1 — Load

Press Browse and pick the folder holding the measurements, or type or paste the path and press Enter; either way the folder is scanned at once and the readable files are listed in the three drop-down menus. Scan folder re-reads a folder whose contents have changed since. Choose one of the three mounts: the other two are then filled in automatically, because the three scans of a sample normally differ in a single token of the file name, so DBB_17_PW_air.xrdml identifies DBB_17_PW_eg.xrdml and DBB_17_PW_heat.xrdml. It works from whichever mount is chosen first and in whichever format the files are held; a line beneath the menus reports what was matched, and says so when a mount is missing from the folder. Press Load.

The tokens recognised are air, airdried, airdry, ad and lutro for the air-dried mount; eg, egl, gly, glyc, glycol and ethylenglykol for the glycol-solvated one; and heat, heated, ht, 350, 500 and 550 for the heated one. A token counts only where it stands as a word of its own, delimited by an underscore, hyphen, dot or space or ending the name — otherwise the ad of Bad_Segeberg would name an air-dried mount — and the rest of the name must agree exactly, so DBB_17_air finds DBB_17_eg and never DBB_17_PW_eg. Files of the format chosen are preferred, so a folder holding both XRDML and .xy exports of everything does not yield one of each. Any assignment can be overridden by hand, and a box already holding a mount of the same sample is left untouched.

Why Browse opens a dialog and not a web page's file picker. A browser cannot tell a page where a folder is. Its file input element reports the names and contents of what is chosen and never the location, which is a deliberate part of the sandbox rather than an oversight, and no amount of scripting gets a path out of it. What makes a chooser possible here is that ClayQuant's server is the analyst's own computer: the process answering the page opens the operating system's own dialog and reads the answer directly. Two consequences follow. The dialog is the one belonging to the machine running ClayQuant, so where the page has been opened from another computer the button says so and declines rather than opening a dialog on an empty desk. And it needs tkinter, which the Windows and macOS installers from python.org include but many Linux distributions package separately as python3-tk; without it the button reports that and the path is typed instead. Nothing else in ClayQuant depends on it.
Paths under WSL. If ClayQuant runs inside WSL while the measurements sit on the Windows side, a path copied from Explorer such as C:\Users\you\samples\TM refers to a drive Linux does not have: Windows drives appear under /mnt, so that folder is /mnt/c/Users/you/samples/TM. Either form may be typed — a drive letter is translated automatically, surrounding quotes are stripped, and a \\wsl$\Distro\home\you share is mapped back to /home/you. The folder that was actually opened is named in the confirmation, so it is visible which one was used.

The point count, angular range and step are reported for each mount. Check that all three cover the same range: the diagnostics compare mounts point by point after interpolation, and a mount measured over a different range will still work but will restrict the comparison.

5.3 Step 2 — Zero error

The 2θ zero error is determined on the quartz 100 reflection, d = 4.2551 å, 2θ = 20.859° for Cu Kα1. This reflection is chosen because no clay basal reflection falls on it.

Find peak automatically locates it and sets the slider; the slider itself steps in 0.01°, half the usual measurement step, and the merit curve beneath shows the figure of merit against candidate offsets so the chosen value can be seen to be the optimum. Each mount carries its own zero error, because each is a separately prepared slide with its own displacement; set all three.

Quartz 100 is only 0.4° from the kaolinite 020 band at 4.36 å. In a clay separate quartz is often weak while kaolinite is strong, and a wide search window will find kaolinite and return a zero error of about −0.4°, displacing the whole pattern. The search window is therefore deliberately narrow (±0.30° by default) and a signal-to-noise test is applied. Where quartz is genuinely absent the program reports that it found no calibration peak and leaves the shift at zero rather than returning a meaningless number; set the value by hand or calibrate on another reflection. See §A.5.

5.4 Step 3 — Background

Choose a model and adjust it until it follows the background without cutting into the peaks. The components are described in §6; the 1/x term, which describes the low-angle rise from air scatter and the direct beam, can be added to any of the others. A non-parametric peak-stripped background is also available for backgrounds no low-order function follows.

Models are fitted not to the raw counts but to a peak-stripped estimate of the background, then refined asymmetrically. This matters: a clay pattern has no peak-free points below about 8°, so fitting the raw intensities there drags the background up into the basal reflections and removes the very signal being quantified. Peak stripping errs the other way, underestimating the background beneath a broad strong low-angle reflection, which is the safe direction but means the low-angle background should always be checked by eye.

Sonneveld–Visser is the exception among the components, and is chosen in the same list. It is not a function fitted to a stripped estimate: the eroded curve is the background, as it is in HighScore, so there is no degree to choose and no stripping width — the two parameters are the same two HighScore exposes, granularity and bending factor, and the panel shows those instead. The 1/x term is not offered with it either, and not for want of arithmetic: the erosion returns a convex background exactly as it found it, and the low-angle rise from air scatter and the direct beam is convex, so it is already in the curve and a fitted 1/x on top would count it twice.

Both of those are proposed when the patterns are loaded, read off the glycol mount — the granularity from the width of the broadest reflection that stands above the noise, the bending factor from which value eight mounts' worth of real fits preferred. The line beneath the sliders says what was measured and whether the measurement or a safety limit decided the answer, and a slider moved by hand afterwards is left alone (§A.19).

Which to use is a real choice and not a matter of taste. Measured over 39 patterns, Sonneveld–Visser puts the baseline higher almost everywhere — by a tenth of the intensity range on a diffuse specimen — and on this laboratory's mounts the fitted components on a peak-stripped estimate give a lower Rwp on every mount tried, because what sits immediately above the baseline in an oriented mount is the broad basal intensity being quantified. The other use of it is as a check: the difference between the two, on one pattern at one width, measures how much of the background is a matter of method rather than of measurement, and a specimen where they disagree by more than a few per cent is one whose percentages carry that disagreement (§A.19).

Apply to all mounts uses the same model for the three mounts, which is appropriate when they were measured under identical conditions.

5.5 Step 4 — Main minerals

Point the box at the phase database of §4.3 — typed, or with Browse, which opens the file chooser of the computer running ClayQuant for the same reason the folder button does (§5.2) — and press Search for main minerals. If a reference library has been loaded, every candidate is calculated and fitted in competition with the clay patterns and with each other in a single non-negative least-squares solve, and each is ranked by the share of the pattern it takes. Without a library, the program falls back to matching predicted peak positions, which is a much weaker test (§A.6).

A dialog lists what was found:

Evidence for the following main minerals has been found in the data:

with, for each, its share of the pattern, how many of its expected lines were found, and the best signal-to-noise among them. Phases with a clear share are ticked; the tail at one or two per cent is listed but left unticked, being largely least-squares slack rather than mineralogy.

This is a shortlist for judgement, not an identification. Phases with similar cells — the feldspars, the spinels, dolomite against ankerite — cannot be separated on diffraction evidence alone at these levels, and a database assembled for general laboratory use contains many phases that cannot occur in a sediment. Tick what the sample can plausibly contain. Selected phases are fitted with the clays and reported separately, then removed when the clay percentages are normalised.

5.6 Step 5 — Kaolinite

Kaolinite is identified by the loss of its 7.15 å reflection on heating. Because the two mounts are separate slides with different amounts of material, the comparison is meaningless until they are put on a common scale; the program does this on a reflection that survives heating, by default the illite 10 å reflection, and reports the scale factor used.

The result is the percentage of the 7.15 å area lost. What survives is chlorite 002, which occupies the same position and does not collapse. A sample with both minerals therefore shows partial collapse, and the surviving fraction is an estimate of the chlorite contribution to that peak.

5.7 Step 6 — Expandable clay

Expandable layers are identified by the shift of the low-angle reflection on glycol solvation: a smectite interlayer takes up a two-layer glycol complex and expands to about 16.9 å. The program locates the reflection in a window of the air-dried and glycolated mounts, reports both positions in ångström and the shift between them, and the ratio of the areas.

A shift towards larger d is the diagnostic. A shift of 13.8 → 16.1 å, for example, is unambiguous evidence of expandable layers. No shift means either that there are none, or that the expandable component is a minor interstratified fraction whose effect is spread through the illite/smectite series rather than concentrated in a discrete peak — which the quantitative fit will still detect.

5.8 Step 7 — Fit and results

Load a reference library, choose the mount to fit — normally the glycol-solvated one — set the angular range, and press Run NNLS fit.

Choose the fitting range deliberately. The lower limit should exclude the direct-beam tail, and 4° is a reasonable default; setting it lower rarely adds information and can let the fit chase background. The upper limit should include the region where the main minerals have their strong lines, so that they are properly determined, but there is little clay information above about 35°.

Restrict orientation parameters limits the fit to library patterns of particular March–Dollase values. Since a well-prepared oriented mount is strongly textured, restricting to the low values (0.1–0.3) both speeds the fit and prevents it from using near-random patterns to model what is really a texture effect.

The results appear as four plots and two tables, described in §8. Export tables and plots writes them to disk.

Read the plots, not only the table. The fit will always return numbers. Whether they mean anything is visible in the difference curve of the Fit plot and in whether the per-phase curves of the All phases plot sit under real features of the measurement. A large systematic residual at one strong peak usually means a layer spacing or crystallite thickness outside the range the library spans (§9).

5.9 The simulator

The simulator drives the calculation directly, independently of any measurement, for teaching, for exploring what a given composition looks like, and for checking the effect of a parameter. It computes a single interstratified or discrete pattern from the controls of §6 and displays it immediately.

6 Reference: interface controls

Every control is listed below by the tab on which it appears, with the identifier used internally, its default, and its meaning. Sliders show their current value; range sliders have two handles.
