ControlIdentifierDefaultMeaning
Mountzero-mountAir-dried Which mount the slider and the automatic search act on. Each mount has its own zero error.
Calibration reflectionzero-referenceQuartz 100, 4.2551 å The reflection whose known position defines the zero. Quartz 100 clears all clay basal reflections. Quartz 101 (3.3435 å) is stronger but overlaps illite 003.
Zero error (°2θ, steps of 0.01)zero-slider0.00 The offset subtracted from the measured angles. The step is 0.01°, half the usual 0.02° measurement step.
Find peak automaticallyzero-auto— Locates the calibration peak within a narrow window and sets the slider. Reports the signal-to-noise, or states that no calibration peak was found.

6.3 Tab 3 — Background

ControlIdentifierDefaultMeaning
Mountbg-mountAir-driedMount displayed and fitted.
Main componentbg-kindChebyshev Polynomial: Σckuk in the angle scaled to [−1,1]. Chebyshev: ΣckTk(u), better conditioned at high degree and the usual Rietveld choice. Exponential: a single decaying term. Peak-stripped: non-parametric; the stripped estimate is used directly and follows any shape, at the cost of having no parameters.
Degreebg-degree4 Degree of the polynomial or Chebyshev component; degree n contributes n+1 terms. Raise it only as far as the background demands: an over-flexible background follows peaks.
Exponential decay (1/°)bg-decay0.20 Decay constant of the exponential component, in reciprocal degrees.
Add 1/x termbg-inverseon Accumulates c/(2θ+x0) on top of the main component. This describes the low-angle rise from air scatter and the direct beam and can be combined with any of the others.
1/x offset (°2θ)bg-offset1.0 The offset x0, which keeps the term finite as the angle approaches zero.
Granularity (points per interval)bg-granularity 0–50, read from the glycol scan Sonneveld–Visser only. Its starting value is proposed from the glycol mount when the patterns are loaded, from the width of the broadest reflection standing above the noise (§A.19); the line beneath the sliders says what was measured and what decided the answer. Moving either slider afterwards is not undone. Points between the samples the erosion runs on — the paper's every twentieth point, and HighScore's parameter of the same name, recommended there between 15 and 30. It is the parameter that decides the baseline, because it sets how wide a feature is removed: 2.2 × granularity × step × √passes, which the panel reports in degrees beneath the slider. Counted in points rather than degrees, as both the paper and HighScore count it, so the same number reaches further on a coarser scan — 20 points is 2.4° on a 0.01° film scan and 4.0° on this laboratory's 0.0167° step.
Bending factorbg-bending0–100, proposed at 0 Sonneveld–Visser only. How much downward curvature the background may keep; HighScore's slider of the same name, where 0 to 2 is the usual advice. 0 allows only a straight or convex background, which is the paper's first form; 1 is the value the paper itself used. On clay patterns 0 to 4 moves the baseline by well under 1 % of the intensity range and 0 to 100 by 2.3–12.4 %, against granularity's 30 % (§A.19). Set granularity first, and note that every mount tested fitted best at 0.
Stripping width (°2θ)bg-snip4.0 Width of the widest feature the stripping treats as a peak. The components are fitted to the stripped estimate and follow it to a few counts, so this control, not the choice of component, is what decides where the background lies. Set it just above the width of the broadest reflection to be kept: narrower leaves peak wings standing in the background and eats into the reflections. It does not control the low-angle tail, which is convex and is therefore preserved at any width (§A.11). Measured over eleven mounts the fit flattens by about 4°, which is the default.
Apply to this mount / Apply to all mountsbg-apply, bg-apply-all— Stores the fitted background. All uses the same model for the three mounts, appropriate when they were measured under identical conditions.

Reading the plot. Four curves are drawn: the measured pattern in grey, the background model as a thick orange line, the peak-stripped estimate as a blue dashed line drawn over it, and the subtracted result in green. The dashes should lie on the orange line; where they part, the chosen components cannot follow the shape of the background and the degree or the component should be changed. The blue curve is the quantity the stripping-width slider controls, and the one the model is fitted to.

Reading the status line. It reports how closely the model follows the stripped estimate, in counts, overall and over the lowest degree separately, and then what the model leaves at the low-angle end: the background value at the first measured point, the measurement there, and the difference as a percentage. That difference is the intensity the fit will be asked to explain as diffraction, and on a scan that opens on the direct-beam tail it should be small - a few percent. A large share there means the background is not following the tail. A goodness-of-fit figure is deliberately not reported for the background: it is close to unity for almost any choice, because the estimate is smooth and the model has several free terms, and it would read as success while the background sat a thousand counts below the measurement at 3°.

7 Reference: command line

There are three commands, and three ways to reach each of them. The ./clayquant script in the project directory (clayquant.ps1 on Windows) is the one that needs nothing set up: it locates the virtual environment itself and runs the module, so it works whether or not the environment is activated and whether or not the installed command was ever written.

From the project directoryWith the environment activatedAs a module
./clayquant build-libraryclayquant-build-library python -m clayquant.library
./clayquant import-structuresclayquant-import-structures python -m clayquant.bern
./clayquant guiclayquant-gui python -m clayquant.gui.app

Options are identical in all three forms; the tables below list them once.

“No module named clayquant”, or a command not found. Both mean the shell is not using the virtual environment. A bare python is then the system interpreter, which has never heard of ClayQuant, and the installed commands are not on PATH. Either activate the environment (source .venv/bin/activate) or use ./clayquant, which does not need it. The error names the interpreter it used — /usr/bin/python rather than something under .venv is the symptom.
A second reason a command can be missing. The installed commands are written into the environment when the package is installed, and at no other time. Updating the source — git pull — therefore does not create a command that the new version has added: the environment keeps the set it was built with, and the new command is reported as not found although its code is present in the checkout. Running ./install.sh (or install.ps1) again writes them all; it lists every command it has checked and names any that is missing rather than reporting success. ./clayquant is unaffected either way, since it runs the module rather than the command.

8 Output files

Export tables and plots writes seven files into the chosen folder.

FileContents
clayquant_mounts.htmlThe three mounts overlaid: air-dried, glycol-solvated, heated. The plot in which the kaolinite collapse and the glycol expansion are seen directly.
clayquant_fit.htmlThe measurement, the fitted curve and the difference, with Rwp in the title.
clayquant_phases.htmlThe measurement with every fitted phase drawn separately, and their sum.
clayquant_clay_phases.htmlThe same for the clay minerals alone, annotated with the clay share of the whole pattern.
clayquant_all_phases.csvQuantification over all fitted phases.
clayquant_clays_only.csvQuantification over the clay minerals alone, renormalised to 100 %.
clayquant_curves.csvThe numerical curves: 2θ, measured, fit, and one column per phase, so the figures can be redrawn in any other program.

The figures are self-contained HTML: they need no plotting software to open and keep the zoom and hover of the interactive versions.

8.1 Columns of the quantification tables

ColumnMeaning
phasePhase name. Interstratified series appear as I/S and C/S, summed over the individual library patterns that contributed.
groupclay or main. Determines which phases the clay-basis normalisation keeps.
coefficientSum of the fitted scale factors cp of that phase's patterns. Depends on the arbitrary normalisation of the library and is meaningful only in comparison within one fit.
scattering_percentThe phase's share of the calculated integrated intensity. The primary number.
amplitude_percentThe phase's share of the summed scale factors.
entriesThe individual library patterns that took non-zero coefficients, naming the composition, orientation parameter, crystallite thickness and layer spacing selected. This is where the fit reports what it found: an I/S share carried by 0.90/0.10 patterns at d = 9.95 å and N = 50 is a specific mineralogical statement.

Each file carries a header recording the measurement, Rwp and Rp, the basis of normalisation, the clay share of the whole pattern where applicable, and a statement that the percentages are shares of diffracted intensity and not weight percent, so that a file cannot later be mistaken for a mass analysis.

9 Limitations

These are properties of the method, not defects to be worked around. Each is stated with its practical consequence.

  1. A fixed library cannot refine. Peak positions, widths and orientation are sampled at the values the library was built with. A specimen whose layer spacing or crystallite thickness falls outside the spanned range will fit badly, and the misfit appears as a systematic residual at a strong peak rather than as an obviously wrong answer. Widen the spanned ranges and rebuild if this is seen.
  2. Percentages are shares of intensity, not of mass (§2.13).
  3. Kaolinite polytypes are not distinguishable from basal reflections (§2.3). A division of intensity between 1M and 2M is not a polytype determination.
  4. The non-basal contribution of an interstratified phase is approximated by that of its host (§2.12). Turbostratic hk bands are not modelled with their true sawtooth profile. The approximation is good for a strongly oriented mount and degrades as r → 1.
  5. Only two-component interstratifications are treated. Three-component systems, and mixed-layer chlorite/smectite/illite, are outside the model.
  6. Accompanying minerals of similar cell cannot be separated. The screen ranks candidates by explained intensity, which is far sharper than position matching, but the feldspars, the spinels and the rhombohedral carbonates remain close enough that the ranking should be read as a shortlist for judgement (§5.5).
  7. The zero error requires quartz. Where quartz is absent the program declines to report a value; it must then be set by hand, and an error there displaces the whole pattern and corrupts the fit.
  8. The low-angle background is the weakest part of the reduction. There are no peak-free points below about 8°, so the background there is an extrapolation. It should always be inspected by eye, particularly when a smectite 001 near 5.2° is at issue.
  9. The ordered case is implemented but not spanned by the default library (§2.7). Regularly interstratified minerals such as rectorite and corrensite will not be fitted correctly by a library built with the default settings.
  10. No absorption or microabsorption correction is applied. For an infinitely thick specimen in Bragg–Brentano geometry the absorption factor is independent of angle and cancels in relative intensities; a thin mount violates this, as does a specimen of strongly contrasting absorption between phases.
