Appendix A — Record of verification tests

This appendix records the tests by which ClayQuant was verified during development: what each test was for, how it was done, what it returned, and what was concluded. Several tests are recorded that failed and led to a change in the program; these are the more informative ones and are reported in full.

On the measurements used. Development was verified against 33 measurements of eleven clay separates from a working laboratory. Those measurements are proprietary and are not reproduced here, nor distributed with the program. They are referred to below as Specimen 1, Specimen 2 and so on, and only derived quantities — agreement factors, peak widths, fitted positions — are quoted, never the measured data themselves.

A.1 The interstratification model against closed-form results

Reasoning. The matrix method of §2.5 is the core of the program and is easy to implement subtly wrongly: the phase convention of equation (2.10) can be transposed, the pair counting of equation (2.11) can be off by one, and the stationary distribution can be inconsistent with the transition matrix. None of these produce obviously absurd output — they produce a plausible pattern that is wrong. The model must therefore be tested against cases whose answer is known independently.

Method and results. Twenty-five tests (test_mixed_layer.py):

TestReasoningResult
Single component reproduces the Laue interference function, for N = 1, 2, 5, 17 With one layer type the general result must collapse to the closed form (2.7). This checks the phase convention, the pair counting and the N-dependence simultaneously, against an exact expression. Agreement to numerical precision at all four thicknesses. Pass.
Two identical layer types behave as one Setting A and B to the same layer must give the one-component answer whatever the proportions, which tests that the two components are combined without double counting. Identical to the single-component calculation. Pass.
A pure end member ignores the absent layer At WA = 1 the pattern must not depend on what B is. A failure here would show the absent component leaking through the transition matrix. Independent of the B layer model. Pass.
Single-layer crystallites show no interference At N = 1 the intensity must be the layer structure factor squared, with no interference term at all. This isolates the pair sum. Reduces to ΣWm|Fm|2. Pass.
Intensity is non-negative — 15 cases: random, ordered and segregated stacking at WA = 0.05, 0.2, 0.5, 0.8, 0.95 Intensity is a squared modulus and cannot be negative anywhere. A sign error in the real part of the matrix sum, or an inconsistent stationary distribution, shows up as small negative excursions between peaks. This is the most sensitive cheap test of the whole formalism. Non-negative throughout in all 15 cases. Pass.
CSDS pair weights G(n) of equation (2.14) must equal 1 at n = 0 and decrease monotonically to zero, or the thickness distribution is misapplied. As specified. Pass.
The random transition matrix is the Markov special case Building a matrix with PAB = WB through the general Markov constructor must give exactly the random one. This checks the constructor against its own special case. Identical matrices. Pass.
Impossible ordering is rejected A PAB implying a probability outside [0,1] is unphysical and must raise rather than silently produce nonsense. Raises. Pass.

Conclusion. The interstratification model reproduces every case for which an independent answer exists, and satisfies the positivity constraint across the full range of composition and ordering.

Consistency of the basal and three-dimensional calculations

Reasoning. The same phase can be computed two ways — as a three-dimensional structure through equation (2.3), or as a one-dimensional layer stack through §2.5. These are independent code paths that must agree on the basal series of a pure phase, otherwise the mixed-layer patterns and the discrete patterns are on different scales and the fit apportions intensity wrongly between them.

Results (test_basal_consistency.py): for illite, chlorite, kaolinite 1M and kaolinite 2M, the basal series computed from the one-dimensional layer model matches the 00l intensities of the full three-dimensional calculation; the derived layer thickness equals d(001) of the cell divided by the number of layers per cell; and the absolute spacings agree with the accepted values (10.02, 14.28, 7.15, 7.15 å). Pass.

Conclusion. The polytype folding of §2.3 is exact for the structures used, and the two code paths are on a common scale.

A.2 Validation against Reynolds (1965)

Reasoning. Everything above is internal consistency: the program agreeing with itself. An external check against a published experiment is needed, and the glycol–smectite complex is the ideal one, because Reynolds (1965) published both his structural model (his Table 1) and his observed and calculated structure factors and intensities for fourteen basal orders (his Table 2). Reproducing his calculated quantities from his stated model tests the layer structure factor of equation (2.6), the scattering factors, the displacement factors and the Lorentz–polarization treatment together, against data that did not come from this program.

Method. The model of his Table 1 was transcribed, the basal structure factors computed from equation (2.6), converted to intensities with the random-powder Lorentz–polarization factor he states he used, normalised at 001, and compared with his Table 2. Agreement is measured by his own reliability factor, R = Σ||Fo|−|Fc|| / Σ|Fo|.

An ambiguity, and how it was resolved. His Table 1 gives occupancies per atomic plane, but the octahedral plane lies on the mirror at z = 0 and is quoted as half its content; and his glycol rows are labelled as half-molecules ("H2C–HO"), which may or may not include their hydrogens. Four readings are possible. Rather than guess, all four were computed and compared with his published values:

ReadingElectrons per cellR(|Fo|)Mean |Δlog10I|
A — octahedral plane as quoted, glycol without H4520.2990.350
B — octahedral plane as quoted, glycol with H4760.3120.327
C — octahedral plane doubled, glycol without H4800.0770.158
D — octahedral plane doubled, glycol with H5040.0390.028

Result. Reading D is correct by a wide margin. It also reproduces independently the electron count Reynolds states for his cell ("about 500 electrons"): 504 against his ~500, where the other readings give 452 to 480. Its reliability factor, R = 0.039, is slightly better than the R = 0.042 he reports for his own best model — as expected, since modern scattering factors are used. Four tests now assert this permanently (test_reynolds_1965.py): the electron count, the reliability factor, the fourteen calculated intensities, and the ordering of the strong orders.

Conclusion. The one-dimensional structure factor calculation reproduces a published experimental analysis to better than its original agreement. This is the strongest external validation in the program, and it simultaneously confirms the choice of Lorentz–polarization factor of §2.8, since no other choice reproduces these intensities.

A.3 Import of a TOPAS structure library

Reasoning. The accompanying minerals enter the fit as calculated patterns, so an error in reading their structures — a misparsed cell parameter, a wrong space group setting, a mis-assigned occupancy — produces a wrong pattern that the fit will nevertheless use. The import must be verified against known diffraction data, phase by phase.

Method and results. A library of 205 phases was imported and the strongest calculated line of each of sixteen well-known phases compared with its accepted position.

PhaseCalculated (°2θ)Accepted (°2θ)Δ
Quartz26.6426.64+0.00
Calcite29.4029.40+0.00
Rutile27.4427.44+0.00
Magnetite35.4335.44−0.01
Halite31.6931.70−0.01
Hematite33.1633.15+0.01
Microcline27.5127.50+0.01
Dolomite30.9430.96−0.02
Albite27.9227.94−0.02
Anhydrite25.4225.44−0.02
Anatase25.3125.28+0.03
Siderite32.0232.05−0.03

Four phases appeared at first to disagree and were examined individually:

  • Barite and fluorite: the calculation was right and the comparison value wrong. Barite's strongest line is 3.10 å (28.74°), not the 3.44 å often quoted from memory, and the full calculated list — 3.445, 3.318, 3.104, 2.835, 2.122, 2.107 å with intensities 98, 63, 100, 53, 81, 56 — matches the powder file essentially exactly. Fluorite's 111 and 220 differ by only a few per cent in intensity and their order is not diagnostic.
  • Gypsum: the calculation gives 4.28 å as strongest where powder files give 7.63 å. This is the well-known preferred-orientation artefact of gypsum powder files, caused by its perfect (010) cleavage; the source library carries an explicit preferred-orientation direction for gypsum for exactly this reason. The calculated random-powder pattern is correct as computed.
  • Pyrite: positions match exactly (3.128, 2.709, 2.423, 2.212, 1.916, 1.634 å); only the relative intensities of 220 and 311 were in question, and published values differ between sources.

Determining the TOPAS origin-choice convention

Reasoning. Thirteen phases failed to import because TOPAS writes the two origin choices of centrosymmetric cubic and tetragonal groups with a trailing letter — Fd-3mS against Fd-3mZ — rather than the :1/:2 of the International Tables. Guessing the mapping was unacceptable: the two origins differ by a translation of (⅛,⅛,⅛), so the wrong choice silently produces wrong intensities for spinels, magnetite, zircon and anatase.

Method and result. The convention was determined from the structures themselves rather than assumed. Diamond, silicon and franklinite, written S, place their 8a site at (0,0,0), which is origin choice 1. Magnetite, spinel, chromite, hercynite and magnesioferrite, written Z, place it at (⅛,⅛,⅛), which is origin choice 2. Zircon (I41/amdZ) has Zr at (0,¾,⅛), the standard choice-2 setting; anatase (I41/amdS) has Ti at the origin, choice 1. Eight independent structures agree: S = origin choice 1, Z = origin choice 2. With this mapping all 205 phases import.

Conclusion. Structure import is verified: positions reproduce accepted values to 0.03° across twelve chemically diverse phases, the four apparent discrepancies are explained and none is an error in the program, and the origin-choice convention is established from evidence rather than assumption.

A.4 Workflow tests on synthetic data

Reasoning. The reduction steps — zero error, background, diagnostics, fit — can only be tested for correctness against data whose answer is known in advance, which no real measurement provides. Synthetic patterns were therefore constructed from the program's own library with a known composition, a known zero error and a known background, and the workflow required to recover them.

TestReasoningResult
Zero error is recoveredA known offset is imposed on a synthetic pattern; the calibration must return it. Tests the peak location and the sign convention — a sign error here would shift every pattern the wrong way.Recovered within the 0.01° step. Pass.
Background with an accumulated 1/x termThe 1/x term must be combinable with any main component, as specified. Tests the design matrix assembly.Recovers an imposed background of that form. Pass.
All background components can be combinedPolynomial, Chebyshev, exponential and 1/x simultaneously — the worst case for conditioning of the linear solve.Fits without degeneracy. Pass.
NNLS recovers a known compositionThe central claim of the method: a synthetic mixture of known proportions must be recovered. Tests the design matrix, the solver and the share computation.Recovers the composition. Pass.
Kaolinite collapse is detectedA synthetic pair with kaolinite removed from the heated mount must be diagnosed as collapse.Detected. Pass.
Chlorite survives heatingThe complement: chlorite must not be reported as collapsed, or every chloritic sample would be called kaolinitic.Survives. Pass.
Smectite swelling is detectedA synthetic pair with the expandable component shifted must be diagnosed as swelling.Detected. Pass.

A.5 File readers and zero-error behaviour on real mounts

Readers

Reasoning. A reader that silently misreads — an offset by one point, a wrong step, an intensity scaling — corrupts everything downstream while appearing to work. The strongest available check is that two independent encodings of the same measurement, the instrument's native XRDML and its own exported two-column text, must agree exactly.

Result. All 33 XRDML files read, and for every specimen where both forms exist the two agree bit for bit: maximum difference 0.000 counts, identical 2θ grids. The instrument configuration carried in the XRDML — wavelengths, goniometer radius, divergence slit, counting time — is also recovered, so a calculation can be set up to match the measurement. An initial version failed on all 33 files because intensities are held in a <counts> element rather than <intensities>; both are now accepted, as are measurements holding several appended scans.

Zero error

Reasoning. The zero error was first determined with a wide search window (±0.6°). Run across all eleven specimens, this produced shifts ranging to −0.40°, with the three mounts of one specimen disagreeing by 0.33°. Mounts of the same specimen are separate slides, so they may differ by a few hundredths of a degree — but not by a third of a degree. The disagreement itself was the evidence that something was wrong.

Diagnosis. Inspecting the region directly showed that in the kaolinite-rich specimens there is no quartz 100 peak at all, and the routine was locking onto the kaolinite 020 band at 4.36 å, 0.4° away. Quartz 100 clears every clay basal reflection, which is why it is the standard choice, but it does not clear the kaolinite hk bands.

Result after correction (narrow window, signal-to-noise test):

SpecimenAirGlycolHeatedSpread
1−0.06−0.06−0.040.02
2−0.06−0.06−0.060.00
3−0.04−0.05−0.050.01
4−0.04−0.06−0.060.02
5−0.04−0.04−0.040.00
6−0.05−0.03not found0.02
7−0.02+0.04not found0.06
8−0.06+0.00−0.060.06
9−0.05+0.06not found0.11
10, 11no calibration peak in any mount—

Conclusion. Detected shifts now lie between −0.06° and +0.06°, are consistent between the mounts of a specimen to 0.02° in the majority of cases, and are of the magnitude expected for instrument zero and specimen displacement. The eight mounts in which quartz is genuinely absent now report that fact instead of a fabricated number. This test is the reason the search window is narrow and the signal-to-noise test exists; with the original settings the program would have silently displaced whole patterns by 0.4°.

A.6 Development of the accompanying-mineral search

Reasoning. Searching a 205-phase database for the few minerals actually present is a discrimination problem, and a method that reports everything is worthless. Each candidate method was tested on a synthetic pattern of known content — quartz, calcite and albite in known proportions — so that false positives could be counted, and then on a real specimen.

MethodReasoningResultVerdict
1. Per-peak window, 2 % cell allowance The obvious first approach: allow each expected line to be found anywhere within the tolerance implied by a 2 % cell deviation. 190 of 205 phases scored 100 % on a three-phase pattern. A 2 % allowance is a window up to 1.6° wide at high angle; on a peak-rich pattern nearly every phase finds something near every expected line.Rejected.
2. One coherent cell scaling + cosine similarity A real cell deviation stretches the whole lattice together, so all of a phase's lines must move by the same relative amount — a far stronger constraint than independent windows. Intensity agreement was added as a cosine similarity. Better: the three true phases ranked 2nd, 4th and 7th. But 157 phases still passed, and graphite, aluminium, copper and lead ranked at the top. A cosine similarity is dominated by whichever single line falls on the largest peak, so any phase with one reflection near a strong peak scores ≈1.Insufficient.
3. Coherent scaling + proportionality + minimum line count Replace the cosine by a test that the implied scale is consistent across lines, and require a phase to have enough lines in range to be judged at all. Improved, but on a real specimen still ranked quartz 56th of 205, behind ilmenite, pyrite, cementite and faujasite — while quartz was demonstrably present, being the zero-error standard.Insufficient.
4. Competitive non-negative least-squares screen Ask the question that actually matters: does this phase explain intensity that nothing else can? Every candidate is fitted simultaneously with the clay library and with every other candidate, and ranked by the share of the pattern it takes. On a real specimen, two phases take four to five times the share of the pattern that the next candidate down takes, and the gap between them and the rest is clean rather than graded; on a second specimen, three phases separate from the rest the same way. Adding the identified phases to the fit lowered Rwp. Adopted.

Conclusion. Position matching cannot discriminate phases in a peak-rich pattern at these levels; explained intensity can. Method 4 is the default whenever a reference library is loaded, and method 3 is retained only as a fallback for when one is not. The residual tail at 1–2 % is least-squares slack rather than mineralogy, which is why the confirmation dialog leaves it unticked.

A.7 Crystallite thickness against measured peak width

Reasoning. The first fits to real specimens gave Rwp near 68 % while reproducing every peak position correctly, with the difference curve showing sharp excursions at the peaks — the signature of a width or position mismatch rather than a wrong phase. Crystallite thickness is the principal control on basal width (§2.6), so it was measured.

Method and results. Full widths at half maximum were measured on a real glycol-solvated mount and compared with the Scherrer prediction:

Position (°2θ)FWHM (°)Assignment
8.820.117illite 001
12.450.134kaolinite 001 / chlorite 002
17.750.134illite 002
26.570.134quartz 101 / illite 003

A width of 0.117° at 8.82° implies a crystallite thickness of about 680 å, or 68 layers. The library in use had been built with a mean of 10 layers, which predicts a 001 width of 0.79° — nearly seven times too broad.

Consequence. Crystallite thickness became a spanned library dimension (§3.3). Rebuilt with means of 5, 15 and 50 layers, the fit selected the N = 50 patterns for the sharp illite, confirming the mechanism.

An instructive negative result. Spanning thickness alone did not improve the agreement: Rwp went from 70.8 % to 70.8 %. The fit now had patterns of the right width available and chose them, but something else was still wrong — which led directly to the next two tests. Had the thickness test been taken as sufficient, the real causes would have been missed.

A.8 Layer spacing

Reasoning. With widths now correct, the residual remained concentrated at one place: the illite 001. At that point the measurement showed 7764 counts where the fit gave 1279 — the strongest clay reflection in the pattern almost entirely unexplained. A peak that is present in both but not fitted is a position problem.

Method and results. The basal spacing was determined from the measurement itself, using two orders so that the result is self-checking:

OrderObserved position (°2θ)d (å)Implied d(001) (å)
0018.8849.94599.946
00217.8084.97689.954
003 (apparent)26.6313.344510.034 — discard

The 001 and 002 agree on d(001) ≈ 9.95 å. The third order appears to disagree, but that reflection is quartz 101 at 3.3435 å overlapping illite 003, not illite alone — a reminder that the 3.34 å peak of a clay pattern is rarely a clay peak only.

The library value, taken from the ICSD illite structure, is 10.022 å, placing the 001 at 8.816° against the observed 8.884°. The discrepancy of 0.066° is half a peak width. Scanning the spacing:

d(001) assumed (å)001 calculated (°)Observed − calculated (°)
9.9008.920−0.038
9.9508.886−0.004
9.9808.853+0.029
10.0008.836+0.046
10.022 (library)8.820+0.062

Conclusion. The specimen's illite has d(001) = 9.95 å, not the 10.022 å of the reference structure. This is not an error in either: illite basal spacing varies from about 9.95 to 10.10 å with interlayer potassium content and hydration, and a single refined structure is one point in that range. Layer spacing therefore became a second spanned library dimension. On rebuilding, the fit selected d = 9.95 å of its own accord, and the illite 001 residual resolved.

A.9 The weighting of the fit

Reasoning. With widths and spacings now spanned, agreement was still poor. The remaining suspect was the fit's own weighting, which had been taken from the background-subtracted intensity. That is wrong on statistical grounds: the variance of a counting measurement is set by the number of photons recorded, and subtracting a smooth background does not reduce it. Weighting by the subtracted value gives near-zero-intensity points — the flat regions between peaks, which are pure noise — the largest weights, and the peaks the smallest.

Result. Changing the weights to 1/max(raw counts, 1), and weighting the solve as well as the metric:

WeightingRwpRp
By background-subtracted intensity (incorrect)70.8 %48.2 %
By raw counts (counting statistics)56.0 %46.4 %

Conclusion. A 15-point improvement in Rwp from a change that alters no physics at all, only the statistical weighting. The lesson is general: when a background-subtracted pattern is fitted, the weights must still come from the counts that were actually measured.

A.10 Cumulative effect and the final state

Reasoning. The preceding tests each addressed one cause. Their cumulative effect on a single real specimen records what each was worth, and whether the final state is fit for use.

StageRwpChange made
Initial68.4 %—
+ thickness spanned70.8 %no improvement alone (§A.7)
+ correct weighting56.0 %§A.9
+ quartz in the fit53.4 %accompanying minerals matter
+ quartz, albite, calcite49.1 %—
+ layer spacing spanned35.7 %§A.8
+ minerals from the competitive screen33.2 % §A.6
These figures predate the background correction of §A.11. They are kept because each row records what one change was worth, and the ordering of the rows is unaffected; the absolute values are not comparable with the measurements below, which were made after it. A background that cut under the data inflated the observed intensity, and Rwp is measured against that intensity, so the earlier figures were flattered by it.

Across all eleven specimens, after the correction. Fitting each glycol mount with the clay library, the accompanying minerals from the competitive screen and the zero error applied, Rwp runs from 37.4 % to 67.5 % with a median of 44.8 %. Eight of the eleven fall between 37 % and 50 %. Two kaolinite-dominated separates fit at 65 % and 68 %; their 7.17 and 7.37 å pair is not matched by the kaolinite library and the cause is not established. Both are specimens in which quartz is absent, so their zero error had to be left unset.

Conclusion. Typical agreement is Rwp ≈ 40–48 %, which is modest for a whole-pattern fit and is what a fixed library that cannot refine positions or widths continuously can be expected to give; it is poor by the standards of a Rietveld refinement, which can refine them. Two specimens of eleven are fitted badly. The plots exist so that this is visible to the user in every case, and §9 states the limitation plainly.

A.11 The peak stripping, and what it must not remove

Reasoning. The background components are fitted to a peak-stripped estimate rather than to the counts, and on real mounts they follow it to a few counts. The estimate therefore is the background, and the question is what the stripping should leave alone. The answer is not a matter of taste. Where a background is convex, the mean of two symmetric neighbours is never below the point itself, so the SNIP operation - replace each point by the smaller of itself and that mean - leaves a convex background exactly unchanged. The low-angle tail of an oriented mount, air scatter and the shoulder of the direct beam, is such a background. A correct implementation returns it untouched; an implementation that removes it leaves thousands of counts of direct beam behind as signal, to be explained as diffraction by whatever pattern in the library rises at low angle.

Method. A background of the measured shape (1820 counts at 3° falling to 339 at 30°) was constructed and stripped with no peaks present at all, at five widths. There is nothing to strip, so the estimate must return the input. Ten peaks of 400 to 7000 counts were then added and the test repeated.

ImplementationEstimate at 3°, background alone Worst error, background aloneWorst error, with peaks
As released (invented neighbours at the ends)546 1274 counts1270 counts
Corrected (comparison narrowed at the ends)1820 0 counts30 counts

Result. The released implementation removed 70 % of a background that contained no peaks whatever. The cause was at the ends of the scan, where the comparison has no neighbour on one side: the missing neighbour was replaced by the point itself, which on a falling edge puts the mean below the point, so every one of the roughly 120 passes lowered it further and the damage propagated inwards over several degrees. Padding the ends with an extrapolated trend, tried next, was no better - the padding is itself stripped and carries the data down with it - and padding by reflection inverts any peak that lies near the end. Narrowing the comparison to what the data allows, so that the window shrinks towards the ends instead of being filled in, restores the property exactly: with no peaks the estimate is the input to within a count, at every width tested.

What it changes. On a real air-dried mount measured from 3.01°, with a Chebyshev background of degree 4 plus the 1/x term:

2θ3.01°4.0°5.0° 8.85°20.85°34.0°
Measured350526732369 3670983493
Background, as released998973933 831484319
Background, corrected329426502174 1151558381

The released background was a nearly flat line 200 counts above the high-angle floor across the whole pattern - which is how it was reported, as a background that appeared not to respond to any control. It could not respond: the estimate it was fitted to had been flattened before the model ever saw it. Averaged over the quantified range the corrected background is 210 counts higher.

The stripping width now means peak width. With the tail preserved by the convexity property rather than by the choice of width, the control no longer trades the tail against the peaks. Measured over the eleven glycol mounts against the clay library alone, without accompanying minerals or zero-error correction, so the values are higher than those of §A.10 and only the trend is meaningful:

Width (°2θ)Overall Rwp 3–4.5° surviving8–40° Rwp
165.3 %2.2 %64.0 %
260.9 %4.5 %61.1 %
359.6 %5.1 %60.1 %
459.0 %5.1 %59.5 %
658.7 %5.1 %59.2 %
858.6 %5.2 %59.1 %

The share of low-angle counts surviving subtraction is now 5 % at every width from 3° upwards: the tail is background whatever is asked for, which is the property above. What the width still changes is how much of a broad reflection is treated as background, and both metrics flatten by about 4°, which is the default. Below 2° the background is lifted into the peaks and the 8–40° figure, a region containing no tail at all, is 4.5 points worse.

The same defect in the library. Each calculated pattern has its own diffuse continuum stripped before storage (§3.3), by the same routine, and the same end effect left that continuum standing over the first degrees - 21 % of the strongest peak at 3.5° on an I/S 0.80/0.20 pattern. Since it is a calculated pattern, the end can be moved: each is now computed on a grid reaching one stripping window beyond both ends of the stored range and trimmed afterwards, which puts the unreliable zone outside the library entirely. The residual continuum at 3.5° falls to 5 %, with the peaks unchanged to three decimal places. This matters because the measured background and the calculated continuum have to be removed consistently: if one side keeps its low-angle rise and the other does not, the fit is asked to reconcile an intensity that only one of them has.

Conclusion. The property to test for a background estimator is not how smooth its output looks but what it does to a background that contains no peaks. That test is now in the suite (tests/test_background.py), at five widths, along with the requirement that peaks are still removed and that the estimate never exceeds the measurement.

A.12 End-to-end tests of the interface

Reasoning. Unit tests cannot show that the assembled program works: state may be lost between steps, a control may not be connected, a computation may be correct but never reach the screen. The complete workflow was therefore driven in a real browser, automatically, on real measurements, with the browser console monitored for errors.

Method. A script loaded three mounts, set the zero error on each, fitted and applied a background, loaded the phase database and reference library, ran the mineral search, confirmed the selection, ran both diagnostics, ran the fit, visited all four result plots, exported, and opened the simulator — capturing a screenshot at each step.

Results. The workflow completed with no JavaScript errors, all four plots rendering and all seven export files written. Two defects were found this way and would not have been found otherwise:

  • The confirmation dialog accepted itself. Dash fires callbacks once for newly created components, so the dialog took whatever was ticked by default at the instant it appeared — the analyst never saw it, and three implausible minerals were silently added to the fit. The screenshot showed the selection already made. Fixed by guarding against the initial invocation.
  • Stale server state. An early run reported results from before a change, because the development server does not reload edited code. Subsequent runs restart the server explicitly.
  • Two curves in the same colour. The background plot drew the measured pattern in the colour of the mount and the subtracted result in a fixed green — which for the glycol-solvated mount is the same green. The two lay on top of each other, the stripped estimate was a faint grey dotted line beneath the model, and a correctly applied background was indistinguishable from none at all; it was reported as the background not being applied. The traces now have fixed, distinct colours and the estimate is drawn over the model rather than under it.
  • Tabs that did not refresh. The interface is built once at start-up, so the background and zero-error views were still showing "not loaded" after the patterns had been read, and kept a background fitted to uncorrected angles after the zero error was set, until some control was touched. Both now take the load and zero-error status as inputs.

Conclusion. The assembled program works end to end on real data. The dialog defect in particular was invisible to unit testing, being a property of the interface framework rather than of any function, and was caught only by driving the interface and looking at what it displayed.

A.12.1 A name that was never imported

What happened. Pressing Load database on the main-minerals tab reported name 'resolve_user_path' is not defined. The function exists and is correct; the module that calls it never imported it. Python raises that only when the line runs, so the interface started, the first three tabs worked, and the fault waited on a button. The same import was missing for the two other calls in that file — loading the reference library and exporting the results — so three of the seven steps were broken in the same way and by the same omission.

Why the existing tests did not catch it. The unit tests exercise the library, not the interface, and the end-to-end browser run that would have caught it had last been made before those three calls were written. A test that only proves what it reaches cannot prove what it does not.

What was added. Two things, because they fail differently. A whole-source check for names that do not exist (tests/test_no_undefined_names.py, using pyflakes) runs over every file in a fraction of a second and finds this class of fault wherever it is, including on paths no test reaches; run against the unfixed source it named all three lines. And the browser run now covers every tab and every button through to the export, which is what establishes that the assembled program works rather than that its parts do.

Result of that run. Load, zero error (−0.06°), background, phase database (209 phases), mineral search, kaolinite (most of the 7.15 å area collapsed on heating, as it should), expandable, library (1601 patterns), fit (Rwp = 49.6 %), export (7 files) and the simulator, with no JavaScript errors.

A.12.2 A step that looked like it did nothing

What happened. Search for main minerals was reported as doing nothing. It was doing exactly what it should, and finishing: the search takes seven to ten seconds, and Dash displays nothing at all while a callback runs. A button that shows no change for ten seconds cannot be told apart from a button that is broken, and was not.

What was changed. Every pane a slow step writes into is now wrapped so that a spinner appears over it while the step is computing, with the previous contents dimmed underneath rather than blanked, and a short delay before it shows so the quick steps do not flicker. That covers the mineral search, the quantification, the library load and build, and the export — the four steps measured in seconds rather than milliseconds.

StepTime on a real measurement
Mineral search, peak matching (no library loaded)7.4 s
Mineral search, competitive fit (library loaded)9.6 s
Quantification over 1614 patternstens of seconds

And the sliders. Each slider carried a bubble showing its value under the handle, which sat on top of the label of the control beneath it and hid part of the text. The value is already shown in the box beside every slider, so the bubbles are removed — nineteen of them.

A.14 Weight percent from the calculated masses

Reasoning. The chain from a fitted scale factor to a mass has four links — the pattern is calculated for one unit of the phase, stored divided by a normalisation, fitted with a coefficient, converted back with the mass of that unit — and an error in any one of them scales a phase without looking wrong. Nothing in a real measurement can catch that, because the true answer is not known. A specimen built out of the library's own patterns, from masses chosen in advance, can.

Method. Known masses of four library patterns were combined into one pattern, multiplied by an arbitrary constant standing for the instrument, and fitted. The fit is exact by construction (Rwp < 10−6), so anything wrong in the result is the conversion rather than the fit.

PhaseMass put inWeight % returned
Illite40.0 %40.00 %
Kaolinite 1M25.0 %25.00 %
Chlorite20.0 %20.00 %
Illite/smectite 0.80/0.2015.0 %15.00 %

Result. Exact to the printed precision, and unchanged when the arbitrary constant is doubled — counting twice as long does not change a weight percent. Equal masses of chlorite and kaolinite come back equal although their shares of scattered intensity differ, which is the point: the conversion uses the mass of the calculated unit and not the intensity. A library that does not record those masses reports no weight percent at all rather than a number computed from something else.

And what it did not test. That the relation was the right one. The specimen was built by inverting ClayQuant's own conversion, so a factor missing from both sides cancelled and the test passed. One was missing: equation (2.25) needs the volume of the calculated unit as well as its mass, and it was implemented with the mass alone.

What caught it

A TOPAS refinement of the same oriented air-dried mount, made independently in the laboratory the measurements come from. The version of it available at the time quantifies four phases — quartz, albite, kaolinite 2M and sekaninaite — and fits illite and chlorite as structureless hkl_Is phases with no weight at all, which is itself worth noting: an expert refinement of an oriented mount does not attempt to weigh the clays either.

The specimens are laboratory material and their compositions are not reproduced in this manual. What is given below is the ratio of ClayQuant's answer to the reference's, which is what a verification record needs and which says nothing about what the specimen contains.
PhaseCell volume ClayQuant / reference, without V ClayQuant / reference, with V
Quartz113 å31.81 1.10
Albite664 å30.39 1.38
Kaolinite657 å30.20 0.35
Sekaninaite1551 å30.40 3.2

Quartz has the smallest cell of the four and was over-weighted against albite by 4.7 times, which is the ratio of their cell volumes, 5.9, to within the other differences between the two analyses. With the volume included, quartz and albite agree with the refinement to 10 % and 38 % where they were out by factors of two and five — and the same correction cuts the quartz of the glycol-solvated mount of that specimen by two thirds, leaving the clay minerals carrying most of the mass, which is what a clay separate should look like.

Two differences remained and were not explained by this: kaolinite at a third of the refined value and sekaninaite at three times it. A later version of the refinement accounts for both, and is described next.

The refinement that weighs every phase

The refinement above was superseded by one of the same measurement in which illite and chlorite are modelled as structures rather than as hkl_Is peak sets, every phase carries a refined March–Dollase parameter instead of a fixed one, and all seven phases are weighed to a sum of 100 %. It is the better reference in every respect, and it changes the earlier comparison as much as it confirms it. Kaolinite and albite both fall by more than half once their texture is refined rather than assumed absent, which is where two of the disagreements above went; and rutile — which ClayQuant had been finding, and which was suspected of being a false positive — is in it as a phase of a few per cent.

PhaseClayQuant / reference Reference r, relative to ClayQuant's
Quartz0.61both fixed at 1
Chlorite (clinochlore)0.88 within a factor of 1.8
Kaolinite0.50slightly more textured
Albite3.20textured about 0 2 0, which ClayQuant cannot express
Rutile0.89 textured about 1 1 0, which ClayQuant cannot express
Illite7.8far more textured than the fit chooses
Sekaninaite11 textured about 2 0 0, which ClayQuant cannot express

ClayQuant's figures are renormalised over these seven phases; the competitive screen also admitted six minerals the refinement does not use — microcline, anorthite, tridymite, thaumasite, a calcium phosphate and pseudoboleite — carrying a further quarter of its mass, and the first three of those sit on feldspar and silica lines. ClayQuant's Rwp for this mount is 36 %, against the refinement's 6.7 %: a fixed library fitted linearly is not a Rietveld refinement and does not pretend to be one.

What this settles. Chlorite at 0.88 and rutile at 0.89 are the first phases to agree with an independent analysis to better than the uncertainty of the preparation, and chlorite could not be compared at all before, since the earlier refinement gave it no weight. Chlorite is counted here as the chlorite and chlorite/smectite entries together, which is what a single clinochlore phase in the refinement corresponds to. Rutile is real.

What it does not. Illite is nearly eight times the refined value and albite three times. Both have an identifiable cause and they are different causes.

Illite is the texture parameter, and the refinement measures it where ClayQuant cannot: it settles on a far stronger texture than the fit here chooses for its illite and illite/smectite entries. Because a basal series has the same shape at every r (§2.9), that difference is invisible in the residual and enters the mass as r3. Holding ClayQuant's illite at the refined value and leaving everything else alone takes the ratio from 7.8 to 3.4 — most of the discrepancy, and exactly the quantity the following section says the measurement cannot determine.

Albite is a limitation of the model rather than of the fit. Its refined texture is about 0 2 0, and sekaninaite's about 2 0 0 — axes that are not c*. ClayQuant applies March–Dollase about c* only, which is right for a platy clay and wrong for a feldspar lying on a cleavage that is not basal, so it has no way to express either texture and assumes both minerals are randomly oriented. Offering the accompanying minerals at several values of r about c* rather than at 1 alone brings albite from 3.20 down to 2.14 and leaves the rest where they were, which is about as much as an axis-restricted correction can do. A general orientation axis per phase is the fix, and it is not implemented.

Expressed as a mass ratio to quartz, which does not move when another phase does, the seven come out at 1.00 for quartz, 0.82 for kaolinite, 1.45 for chlorite, 1.46 for rutile, 5.2 for albite, 12.8 for illite and 18 for sekaninaite. Kaolinite, which looked like a factor-of-two problem in the renormalised table, is the second-best phase on this measure; what moves it is quartz, which ClayQuant under-weights by a third.

What no refinement of this mount can supply. It is the air-dried mount, and it contains no expandable phase: no smectite, no montmorillonite, no illite/smectite. That is not an omission but a consequence of the preparation — in an air-dried specimen an expandable clay sits near 14–15 å, on top of chlorite 001 and vermiculite, and cannot be separated from them. That is what the glycol-solvated mount is for (§2.1). The reference therefore constrains six crystalline phases and the illite, and says nothing about the expandable clay, which is the quantity the three-mount method exists to measure.

How well the fit determines the texture parameter

The illite discrepancy above is mostly the texture parameter, so it is worth measuring what the parameter is worth. For the kaolinite entries of the library, from r = 0.1 to r = 1:

rSimilarity of the stored pattern to r = 1 Mass per unit coefficient
0.10.8423.8 × 10−5
0.50.8614.8 × 10−3
1.01.0003.8 × 10−2

A tenfold change in r changes the shape of the pattern by 16 % and the mass it implies by a factor of a thousand. The shape it changes is the ratio of hkl to 00l intensity, which in a strongly oriented mount is the weakest thing in the pattern. The weight percent of a basal-dominated phase is therefore not merely uncalibrated: it rests on a quantity the measurement barely determines.

That has a consequence for the calibration of §2.13. A factor kp fitted while r is also free would be absorbing a parameter the data cannot fix. The calibration should instead fix r per phase, determined from the specimens of known composition, so that afterwards the fit chooses only how much of each phase is present.

The refinement bears this out from the other side. It determines r for each phase because it fits the hkl reflections as well as the basal ones, in a pattern where those reflections are weak but present; ClayQuant's clay library is basal-only by construction, so nothing in it constrains r at all. Where the two nearly agree on r — chlorite — they agree on the weight to 12 %; where they do not, they disagree by the cube of the ratio.

The importer now checks itself against TOPAS

A structure block written by TOPAS states two numbers ClayQuant does not need, because it works both out from the sites and the cell: cell_mass and cell_volume. That is what makes them worth reading. They are the same two quantities stated independently, by the program the library was written for, so a block that has lost atoms disagrees with itself — and nothing else in the import notices, since a phase with some of its sites is still a phase that reads.

The importer now compares them and reports every phase that disagrees by more than 0.5 %. Over the 209-phase laboratory library exactly one does, and it is the phase that had been added by hand:

phases that were imported but do not match what TOPAS says they weigh:
  Sekaninaite: cell mass works out to 1696.146 from the sites and cell given,
  but the block states 2592.043 (65 % of it); sites are probably missing

Five oxygen sites — O2 to O6 — are absent from that item; they are present in the refinement's own output for the same phase. The cell volume agrees exactly, which localises the fault to the site list rather than the cell. Restoring the five sites brings the computed mass to 2592.090 against the stated 2592.043. The phase is still written to the database, because whether an incomplete structure is usable is the user's judgement and not the importer's; it is only no longer silent. Sekaninaite is a trace phase here, so little followed from it, but the same fault in a major phase would have gone the same way.

Conclusion. A test built by inverting the code it tests will agree with the code and not with nature. Both faults in this section were found by comparison with something that did not come from ClayQuant: the missing cell volume by a refinement of the same measurement, the missing oxygen sites by the refinement's own statement of what the structure weighs. The synthetic test remains, rebuilt from the powder relation rather than from ClayQuant's conversion, alongside a check that the two calculation routes for one phase — as a discrete cell and as the host layer of a stack — weigh a specimen alike.

A.15 A weighed standard, and a random mount ClayQuant cannot fit

Reasoning. The oriented mounts confound two things: whether the conversion from a scale factor to a mass is right, and whether each phase's texture is modelled. A random powder mount removes the second — there is no texture and every phase is fitted at r = 1 — so what remains is the conversion alone. And a random mount can carry a weighed standard, which makes the reference absolute rather than relative. The laboratory's bulk analyses are exactly this: pressed random powders with 20 % of corundum by weight added before mounting, refined in TOPAS.

What the spike says about the reference analyses. The refinements record no trace of the spike — the weight of corundum added is knowledge held outside the files — so their weight percent is relative, normalised to 100 over the phases that were weighed. Applying (2.26) makes them absolute, and the difference from 100 is what each refinement does not account for: its illite and chlorite, which it fits as hkl_Is peak sets carrying no weight, together with any amorphous content. Sixteen refinements, eight specimens each prepared twice:

Quantity, over eight specimensLowestHighest Largest difference between the two preparations of one specimen
Corundum, refined against 20 % added21.0 %44.5 % 2.3 %
Scale factor implied, Wstd/W′std 0.450.950.03
Unaccounted, of the spiked powder4.9 %55.0 % 2.8 %
Unaccounted, of the specimen as sampled6.2 %68.8 % 3.5 %

The per-specimen compositions are laboratory data and are not reproduced here; what the verification argument needs is the spread and the reproducibility. The two preparations of a specimen agree to within 0.6 to 2.8 percentage points on the unaccounted fraction, which is the reproducibility of the whole chain — splitting, spiking, pressing, measuring and refining — and is the figure against which any disagreement should be read. The unaccounted fraction ranges from 5 % to 55 % of the spiked powder, so it is not a correction but the largest single number in several of the analyses.

Note the two bases. A weight percent from (2.26) is a fraction of the powder the diffractometer saw, which is one part standard to four parts specimen; the specimen as it was sampled is the remaining 80 %, so every phase in it, and the unaccounted fraction with them, is larger by 1.25. That is the basis an amorphous content is normally quoted on, and Quantification.original_basis returns it, with the standard removed since it is not part of the specimen.

The test that could not be run

ClayQuant was fitted to the same random mount, over the phases the refinement uses so that phase selection was not part of what was being tested, every phase at r = 1, with the corundum declared as the internal standard. The result is not a usable check, and the reason is worth recording rather than the numbers:

Window8–16°16–24° 24–32°32–40°40–48° 48–56°56–64°64–72°
Rwp94 %60 % 45 %42 %50 %47 % 40 %54 %

Overall Rwp is 43 % against the refinement's 7.6 %, at the best setting found, and the misfit is spread across the whole range rather than concentrated anywhere.

What makes the result unusable is not its size but its instability. Shifting the pattern by the zero error the refinement reports, 0.035°, and then by twice that in each direction, with everything else held fixed:

Shift applied−0.070°−0.035° 0+0.035°+0.070°
Rwp67 %51 % 43 %54 %61 %
Calcite, against the reference0.450.54 0.691.051.32
Quartz0.630.82 0.840.690.56

A tenth of a degree of alignment moves calcite by a factor of three. Nothing about the mass conversion can be read through a sensitivity that large, and the sensitivity has a cause: the reference refinement models a specimen displacement of 0.061 mm, which displaces each reflection by an amount varying as cosθ, and ClayQuant has no such model. No single constant zero error can align peaks across 8–70° in its place, so the fit trades one end of the range against the other and the phase weights follow. Over the 3–40° of an oriented clay mount the same displacement is nearly a constant offset and the zero-error correction absorbs it; over a bulk scan it is not. The other absences compound it — one fixed pseudo-Voigt where the reference convolves an axial-divergence model and a slit width, no sample-transparency correction, and no per-phase cell, size or strain — and 70 % of the weighted misfit lies between the peaks rather than on them, which is the background left over when peaks sit in the wrong places.

The background model is not the cause: Chebyshev degree 4, 6 and 8, with and without an inverse term, change Rwp by 0.2 percentage points and calcite by 0.01. That was worth checking, because it was the first explanation that suggested itself and it was wrong.

Conclusion, and what it does not license. The internal-standard arithmetic is implemented and tested, and the reference analyses above are absolute because of it. But the corundum-spiked mounts do not supply the calibration of §2.13, for two independent reasons, either of which alone would be enough:

  • They are a different material. The spiked mounts are bulk rock powders; the oriented mounts are the fine separate of the same rock. For the specimen of §A.14 both refinements exist, and they settle it directly: calcite and dolomite-ankerite are both major constituents of the bulk, and neither appears in the oriented mount at all, while kaolinite and rutile appear in the oriented mount and in no form in the bulk. The separation removes the carbonate and concentrates the fine, dense accessories, so the composition of one preparation is not the composition of the other, and nothing in either measurement says what fraction of the rock the separate is.
  • The reference refinements leave illite and chlorite unweighed. Even for the bulk rock they give clay plus amorphous as one number — for the specimen of §A.14, a substantial one, reproducible between its two preparations to 2 percentage points — so they do not state the clay composition that kp would be fitted against.

What would supply it is the pairing described in §2.13: the same separate mounted twice, once as a spiked random powder and once oriented. The random mount fixes the composition without texture; the oriented fit of that known composition then yields kp directly. For ClayQuant to fit the random half of such a pair, the shortcomings listed above would have to be addressed first.

A.16 Structures as refined, rather than as published

Reasoning. Every structure the library calculates from is of somebody else's specimen. For quartz that hardly matters; for a clay it may matter a great deal, because the octahedral sheets accept iron for magnesium and for aluminium in proportions that differ from one deposit to the next, iron scatters about twice as strongly as the magnesium it replaces, and the substitution sits at a definite height in the layer — so it changes the basal structure factors, and therefore every basal intensity ratio the quantification rests on. Those occupancies are refinable against a measured pattern. Where a refinement of the same specimen exists, it has already measured them.

What the reference refinement of §A.14 actually refined. Its cells, and seven occupancy parameters across three phases: the two octahedral sites of the illite, four octahedral and two tetrahedral sites of the chlorite, and the Mg/Fe site of the cordierite. No atomic position and no displacement parameter was refined for any phase, so positions and B come from the published structures either way. The chlorite refines to substantially more iron than the published clinochlore carries, and unevenly between its four octahedral sites; the illite takes iron on one of its two sites and none on the other. The values are this specimen's and are not reproduced here.

Two of the seven parameters are worth distrusting rather than using blindly. Both tetrahedral Si/Al parameters of the chlorite refined to a bound, leaving an all-aluminium tetrahedral sheet, which is not a chlorite; silicon and aluminium differ by one electron, so the data cannot separate them and the parameter drifts. It costs little — about 0.7 % of the cell mass and nothing measurable in the pattern — but a parameter at its limit is a parameter the measurement did not determine, and the same is true of the specimen displacement in the same file.

Method. TOPAS writes a refined value back in the syntax it read, so the refinement's output is a structure library and the same importer serves. The clay structures were taken from it, the pattern library recalculated, and the fit of §A.14 repeated. To separate the refined occupancies from the refined cells, a third library was built with the refined sites placed on the published cells.

Structures usedRwp
Published throughout35.9 %
Clays: refined occupancies, published cells31.7 %
Clays: refined occupancies and cells31.2 %
… and the accompanying minerals refined too34.9 %

Result. Taking the clay structures from the refinement improves Rwp by 4.7 percentage points, the largest single improvement recorded in this appendix after the fit weighting of §A.9, and the occupancies account for 4.2 of the 4.7. The agreement ratios of §A.14 barely move: chlorite from 0.94 to 1.08, illite from 7.5 to 7.3, quartz unchanged at 0.6. That combination is coherent rather than disappointing. Rwp measures the shape of the calculated pattern, which the occupancies fix; the weights are governed by the r-degeneracy and by texture axes the model cannot express (§A.14), which a structure cannot touch.

The effect on the calculated basal series, as the cosine similarity of the normalised pattern to the one from the published structure, locates it:

PhaseRefined cell onlyRefined sites only Both
Chlorite0.8260.9610.810
Illite0.9530.9890.947
Kaolinite 2M0.9931.000 0.993

Chlorite moves most, and its 003 — the reflection an octahedral iron content is refined against — falls by a factor of about 2.6 relative to 002. Kaolinite barely moves, which is expected: its occupancies are all 1 and only its cell changed. Note that the cell changes the isolated pattern more than the sites do, while the sites improve the fit more. That is not a contradiction: a changed cell mostly moves the basal peaks, and the library spans layer spacing (§A.8), so the fit absorbs a spacing change by choosing a different spanned entry. A changed intensity ratio it cannot absorb at all.

Why not the accompanying minerals as well

Because it is measurably worse, by 3 points of Rwp, and the phase responsible is quartz: taking quartz's refined cell alone costs 3.0 points, albite's alone 1.3, and rutile's and cordierite's nothing. Quartz is a special case with an identifiable mechanism. It is also the zero-error standard (§5.3), and the standard is a fixed d(100) constant rather than the library's quartz: align the pattern to that constant and then fit a quartz whose refined cell puts its own 100 elsewhere, and the standard and the structure are out of step by 0.027°. Making the standard consistent with the refined cell recovers 1.2 of the 3.0 points. The remaining 1.8 is not explained; the refined quartz cell is simply a worse description of these data than the published one, in a program that cannot re-refine it.

A first hypothesis was that the refined cells carried the refinement's own alignment corrections — it fits a zero error and a specimen displacement, the displacement at its limit, where ClayQuant fits only a constant zero error. It was wrong: removing ClayQuant's zero-error correction makes every case worse, refined and published alike. Recorded because it was plausible and is the sort of explanation that is easier to assert than to test.

Conclusion. Refined clay structures are used where a refinement supplies them, and are the recommended input; the accompanying minerals stay on the library structures unless a library structure is demonstrably wrong, as the incomplete cordierite of §A.14 was. What a refinement cannot supply is the commonest case: an oriented mount refined with its clays as hkl_Is peak sets has no clay structure in it, and the import reports that rather than succeeding emptily. 21 automated tests cover the reading, the name mapping, the substitution inside the loader, and the restoration of the published structures afterwards.

A.17 Against measurements of the pure minerals

Reasoning. Every comparison up to here has been against an analysis of a mixture, where a disagreement can lie in the calculation, in the phase selection, in the texture of one phase among several, or in the reference itself. A measurement of a single pure mineral removes all of that at once. And one quantity in such a pattern is free of the two things a pure mount does not reveal — how much material is in the beam, and how well oriented it is: the ratio of one basal intensity to another. Preferred orientation multiplies a whole basal series by one factor (§2.9), so it divides out completely, and so does the amount of material. What is left in a basal ratio is the structure factors, the Lorentz–polarization factor, the beam-overflow correction and the crystallite thickness distribution.

Method. Oriented air-dried mounts of separate pure clay minerals, measured on one instrument under one setting within fourteen hours: 240 mm radius, graded incident mirror, 0.03 and 0.02 rad Soller slits, fixed 0.5° divergence and anti-scatter slits, 14 mm mask, 0.0167° steps, 19.7 s per step, no attenuator. Each 00l was integrated over ±1.0° of where the layer spacing puts it, after peak-stripped background subtraction, and divided by another order of the same pattern. The calculation used the published structures and the same instrument description, at the crystallite thickness that best matches the measured peak widths.

The integration window is not a detail, and getting it wrong produced a confident and wrong conclusion. A clay basal reflection has a full width at half maximum near 0.1–0.2°, so ±0.35° looks more than ample. It is not. Stacking disorder gives these reflections a long diffuse tail, and on one of the chlorites below a ±0.35° window held only 36–72 % of each order's area — and a different fraction of each order, which is precisely what a ratio of orders is sensitive to. At ±1.0° the same pattern gives 85–93 %. The 005 ratio of that chlorite reads 0.77 at ±0.35°, 1.22 at ±0.6° and 1.34 at ±1.0°. An earlier version of this section reported the ±0.35° figures and drew a conclusion from them that the corrected figures do not support; the retraction is below.
00lKaolinite Chlorite AChlorite B
0011.000.940.99
0021.051.001.00
0030.920.941.18
004—1.341.32
005—1.341.18

Observed divided by calculated, each column normalised on the order shown as 1.00 — 001 for kaolinite, 002 for the chlorites, 002 being the strongest chlorite basal. Integrated over ±1.0°. The 006 of both chlorites is omitted: the calculated 006 falls close to a node of the structure factor, so its ratio is set by noise rather than by the model.

Result. Kaolinite's 002/001 comes back at 1.05, and it is stable against the window: 1.02 at ±0.35°, 1.05 at ±1.0°, 1.08 at ±1.5°. That is the strongest single piece of evidence in this appendix that the chain of §2 is right — an absolute basal intensity ratio of a real mineral, reproduced to about 5 % with nothing fitted. Its 003 is 0.92, having read 0.65 at the narrow window.

Both chlorites come out about 1.3 on 004 and 1.2–1.3 on 005: the calculation under-produces the higher orders, by a similar amount in both specimens. Their 003 differs (0.94 against 1.18), which is the one place they are not alike.

A retraction

Read at ±0.35° and at a crystallite thickness fixed at 25 layers rather than matched to the observed widths, the same two chlorites appeared to depart from the published clinochlore in opposite directions — 0.62 against 0.83 on 003, 0.61 against 0.81 on 005. That looked like strong evidence that the two specimens differ in octahedral iron, that no single structure can serve both, and that a per-specimen composition was needed. Corrected, the two chlorites agree with each other to within 0.02 on 004 and differ from the published structure in the same direction on every order but 003. The pattern is a common shortfall in the calculated higher orders, not a composition difference between specimens, so this data does not call for a per-specimen chlorite composition; the published structure remains the better-supported default.

Fitting the iron content anyway bears that out rather than contradicting it. On these two patterns the two-parameter fit of §4.4 reduces the residual by only 1.5 to 1.7 times, drives one specimen to essentially zero octahedral iron — which for a mineral sold as an iron-rich chlorite is not credible — and settles against the lower bound of the crystallite thickness grid. A parameter at its bound is a parameter the measurement has not determined, and three signs of a model straining to fit are worth more than the improvement in the number being minimised. The mechanism is available and is verified against patterns calculated from known compositions, which it recovers; what these measurements do not show is a need for it.

What the chlorite shortfall is not

The chlorites need their 004 raised by about a third against their 002, and their 005 by a fifth to a third. The obvious suspect is a displacement parameter: exp(−B q2) falls with angle, so a B that is too large suppresses the high orders. The exponential is weak here — at 005 of a 14.28 å spacing q2 is 0.031 å−2, so B = 0.65 costs 2 % of an amplitude — but F(00l) is a sum of terms with opposing signs and the high orders are small differences of large numbers, so the sensitivity does not follow from the size of the exponential and has to be computed. Computed, with the 004/002 ratio the quantity to move from 0.62 to 0.83:

Change made to the calculation004/002 reachedVerdict
Octahedral B from 0 to 6 å2 0.63 → 0.57Ruled out; and the wrong way round
Every B in the structure scaled 0 to 6× 0.64 → 0.55Ruled out
Hydroxyl B from 0 to 8 å2 0.62 → 0.63Ruled out
Fe2+ in place of Fe3+0.62 Ruled out
Interlayer hydroxide sheet moved ±0.3 å along c* 0.48 → 0.57Ruled out, and it destroys 001
Crystallite thickness, 4 to 40 layers0.63 → 0.62 Ruled out (it is the 001 control, not the 004 one)
Single-crystal Lorentz factor instead of the powder one1.25 Overshoots, halves 001, and contradicts §A.2
Beam-overflow specimen length 25 → 15 mm0.62 → 0.80 Reaches it — see below

So the displacement parameters cannot do it. The whole range of 004/002 accessible to any B, at any value from zero to six times the published one, is 0.55 to 0.64, and the direction a shortfall needs is exhausted within 2 % of the published value. Neither can the iron valence, the hydroxide sheet's height, or the crystallite thickness.

The one change that reaches 0.83 is not structural at all: the specimen length in the beam-overflow correction (§2.10), which had been assumed at 20 mm rather than measured. At 15 mm the chlorites' 001, 004 and 005 all land within a few per cent. But the cross-check refutes it. The three mounts were prepared the same way, so one length must serve all three, and it does not:

Specimen length assumed12 mm15 mm 16 mm18 mm20 mm25 mm
Kaolinite0.380.220.18 0.090.0650.065
Chlorite A0.220.140.14 0.190.250.26
Chlorite B0.190.060.050 0.140.210.22

Root mean square of obs/calc − 1 over the orders other than the reference, at the crystallite thickness that best fits each row.

Kaolinite wants 20 mm or more and the chlorites want 15–16, and the disagreement is not marginal: at 16 mm kaolinite's residual triples. The reason the two disagree is worth noting, because it says what the parameter is doing. Kaolinite's reference order and the chlorites' both sit at 12.4°, and 20 mm puts full illumination at 12.0° — so at 20 mm and above the correction has stopped acting on any of these ratios at all, which is why kaolinite's residual is flat there. Shortening the specimen brings the reference order back into the overflow region and lifts the higher orders against it. That lifts the chlorites onto their measured values and lifts kaolinite off its own. A parameter that can absorb one discrepancy while creating another is not the cause of either.

So it remains open. What has not been tested: the individual oxygen and hydrogen heights within the chlorite layer, as against the rigid shift of the whole hydroxide sheet tried above; interstratified smectite or vermiculite layers in a natural chlorite, which would add intensity at low angle and redistribute the orders; and a different chlorite structure altogether. The integration window works against the observed excess rather than explaining it — the measured peaks are broader than the calculated ones, so a finite window discards more of the observation than of the calculation, and the true excess is if anything larger than reported.

What this does not cover. Only kaolinite and the two chlorites are single-phase enough to use. Of the other mounts measured, an illite's strongest reflection is quartz rather than illite, two smectites and a saponite carry several per cent of quartz, a bentonite carries opal-CT, and a synthetic hectorite is close to X-ray amorphous. None of those can serve as a reference for a basal ratio until the accompanying phase is either removed or modelled. All the mounts are also air-dried, while the quantitative fit is made on the glycol-solvated mount (§2.1), so nothing here bears on the expandable clays at all.

And the absolute scale. A basal ratio needs no standard, which is why these figures can be given at all. The absolute scale — the kp of §2.13 — needs one, measured through the same optics. A corundum mount measured alongside these was run with a 0.25° divergence slit where the clays had 0.5°, and with a fixed slit the ratio between two such settings is not a constant: where the beam overflows the specimen both slits illuminate the same area and the ratio is 1, where neither overflows it is 2, and the crossover falls between 2θ = 6° and 12° at a place that depends on the specimen length. That is exactly where the diagnostic basal reflections are — glycol-smectite 001 at 5.2°, chlorite 001 at 6.2°, illite 001 at 8.8°, kaolinite 001 at 12.3°. A standard measured through the clays' own optics avoids putting a modelled factor of up to two across the very peaks the calibration is for. That standard has since been measured, on these mounts' own settings, and §A.18 reports what it gives — including a check on the orientation correction that bears directly on the shortfall left open above.

A.18 A standard through the clays' own optics

Reasoning. Everything in §A.14 through §A.17 is either a ratio or a relative proportion. The one number none of them reaches is the absolute one: how much mass a fitted coefficient stands for in an oriented mount, the kp of §2.13. An internal standard cannot supply it, because a spike does not orient as the clays do (§A.15). An external standard can, because it is never asked to: it is measured on its own, and only the instrument is shared. And on a mount of a pure mineral the answer needs no independent analysis at all — the weight fraction is the purity, so (2.28) has a known answer and kp is the amount by which it misses.

Method. A pressed corundum mount was measured under the settings of the pure clay mounts of §A.17, and the agreement is exact rather than approximate — which matters, because the previous corundum available had a 0.25° divergence slit against the clays' 0.5°, and with a fixed slit that is a factor of up to two placed across the diagnostic low-angle peaks:

SettingCorundumThe four clay mounts
2θ range, step count3.008–39.990°, 2214 3.008–39.990°, 2214
Counting time per step19.685 s19.685 s
Divergence / anti-scatter slit0.5° / 0.5° 0.5° / 0.5°
Mask14 mm14 mm
Tube45 kV, 40 mA45 kV, 40 mA

All five measured within ten days on the same configuration. ExternalStandard.comparable_with compares these fields and reports nothing to flag; on the earlier corundum it named the slit difference.

The mass attenuation coefficients that (2.27) and (2.28) need were computed from each structure's mass fractions and checked against published values for the compounds:

Phaseμ/ρ, cm2/g Published

Quartz34.4534.4
