At Cu Kα, from Hubbell & Seltzer (1995). The elemental table stops where its authors' does: an element it does not hold raises rather than being given a plausible value, and the discontinuity across the Cu absorption edge is preserved — iron is 308 cm2/g and nickel, two places further on, is 49, which is not a typographical error but the reason an iron-rich clay and a corundum cannot be compared without this correction.

Result. Each clay mount was fitted with three-dimensional powder patterns of its own mineral spanning the orientation parameter, so that the mount's own hkl-to-basal ratio determines r rather than leaving it free (§A.14). The weight fraction each mount was credited with is its own purity, from the accompanying phases in the same fit.

MountFitted asW μ/ρRwp rr−3 kp
Kaolinitekaolinite0.8629.77 71 %0.162440.245
Chlorite Achlorite0.9739.36 94 %1.001.00.216
Chlorite Bchlorite1.0039.36 94 %0.683.20.281
Illiteillite0.8142.12 86 %0.594.90.247

Corundum standard: Rwp 41 % over the whole range, 33 % over 20–39°, fitted r = 0.99 as a pressed powder should be. K = 2.28 × 104 in the units of (2.27).

Two things in that table are worth separating. The first is the spread: 0.216 to 0.281, mean 0.247, a relative standard deviation of 11 % and a ratio of extremes of 1.30, across four mounts of three chemically different minerals. Texture, microabsorption and structural error are the three things kp lumps together, and all three differ between these minerals — so a factor they share to within 13 % is not mostly any of them. It is a property of the comparison between a settled clay film and a pressed powder, which is what these four mounts have in common and the corundum does not.

The second is a cross-check that falls out of it, and it is the stronger result. The orientation correction r−3 (§2.9) is the largest single factor in an oriented-mount mass, and across these four mounts it ranges over a factor of 244 — from a near-perfectly plated kaolinite at r = 0.16 to a chlorite that behaves as a random powder at r = 1.00. The mass inferred for each depends directly on it. If the r−3 scaling of mass were wrong, four specimens spanning that range could not land on one factor; they land within 1.30. This is the first evidence in the manual that the orientation correction is right in magnitude and not merely in shape, and it comes from data rather than from the model.

What the missing factor of four is not

The calculation over-produces by 1/0.247 ≈ 4 per unit mass in these mounts. The first suspect is specimen thickness, because (2.28) is derived for a specimen thicker than the beam penetrates and a settled clay film need not be. It is refuted twice over.

Refuted by arithmetic: at the packing density of a settled film the penetration depth sinθ/2μ is 3.5 µm at 6° and 20 µm at 35° for illite, so a deposit of 50 µm returns 100 % of the infinite-thickness intensity below 12° and 88 % at 35°, and 100 µm returns 99 % everywhere. The thinness needed to lose three quarters of the intensity is 1.3–2.2 µm depending on packing — below a single kaolinite booklet's worth of stacking, and far below any mount that survives handling.

Refuted by the data, which is the part that settles it: absorption in a thin film is angle-dependent, and in the direction opposite to what is observed. A film thin enough to give 0.25 at the illite 001 returns 0.071 at 35°, so the higher basal orders would come in a factor of 3.5 low against the first. §A.17 measures the higher orders of two chlorites coming in 20–30 % high. A thin film cannot be the explanation of the absolute deficit and be absent from the ratios at the same time, and the ratios are the better measurement of the two.

What remains, and what would distinguish them:

The irradiated length
The beam-overflow correction (§2.10) is applied with an assumed 20 mm of specimen, for both the clays and the corundum. With a fixed 0.5° slit the beam is 20 mm long at 6° and 30 mm at 4°, so a deposit shorter than the pressed standard loses intensity the correction does not restore. This can reach a factor of two, not four, but it is the one candidate that is a measurement rather than a hypothesis: the physical length of a clay mount's deposit along the beam, against the corundum's.
The deposit's mass per unit area
If the mounts are weighed before and after deposition, the mass in the beam is known outright and kp stops being inferred from a purity at all — (2.28) can be replaced by a direct comparison, and the thickness question above is answered by the same number.
A common factor in the basal calculation
Anything that multiplies a whole basal series by one constant per gram, independent of the mineral, is indistinguishable from the above on this data. It would have to leave the ratios of §A.17 untouched, which most candidates do not.

Why r is fixed rather than fitted, restated with numbers

The same four mounts were run a second way, with the library's own interstratified entries at the pure end member — which carry the crystallite-thickness broadening a powder calculation lacks, and fit far better — leaving r free:

MountRwp, powder Rwp, library kp, r fixed kp, r free
Kaolinite71 %71 %0.2450.245
Chlorite A94 %56 %0.2160.391
Chlorite B94 %40 %0.2810.292
Illite86 %54 %0.2470.100
Ratio of extremes 1.303.90

The better-fitting route gives the worse calibration, by a factor of three in spread. That is the r-degeneracy of §A.14 measured rather than argued: a basal-dominated pattern does not determine r, so a fit free to choose it will trade r against scale at no cost in Rwp and carry the trade straight into the mass. A lower residual is not a better calibration, and this is the clearest case of it in the manual. r belongs to the hkl reflections, and a calibration should be made where they are.

What this does not license

kp remains 1 in the code. Four mounts, one preparation, one operator, one instrument and one standard is a result, not a calibration table, and the factor is an instrument constant that no other laboratory could adopt. Beyond that:

  • Every mount is air-dried. The quantitative fit is made on the glycol-solvated mount (§2.1), so none of this bears on the expandable clays, which are the phases whose texture is least like a chlorite's.
  • The purities used (0.81 to 1.00) come from the accompanying phases in the same fits, so they carry the same modelling error they are meant to correct. The illite's 0.81 is the weakest of them.
  • The powder-route residuals are 71–94 %. A three-dimensional powder calculation with one orientation parameter is a poor description of an oriented mount, and these masses inherit that. The constancy of the factor across four such fits is more informative than any one of them.
  • Smectite has no pure mount here at all, and no calibration.

What it does establish: the machinery is complete and checked — absorption coefficients against published compounds, the conditions of two measurements compared rather than assumed, the infinite-thickness assumption computed rather than hoped for — and applied to real data it returns one factor, not four unrelated ones. When the glycol and heated mounts are measured, the same three commands give kp for those, and the question of whether it is one factor per preparation or one per mineral will be answerable.

A.19 A second background estimator, and what it changes

Reasoning. The background is fitted to a stripped estimate, and §A.11 establishes that the estimate is the background: the components follow it to a few counts, so whatever the estimator decides, the analysis inherits. That makes the estimator the single most consequential choice in the workflow and leaves it untested against anything but itself. A second, independent estimator is the only way to find out how much of the background is measurement and how much is method.

The obvious second choice is the oldest one. Sonneveld & Visser (1975) is the earliest of the iterative-erosion baseline estimators, thirteen years ahead of the SNIP paper and built on the same idea, and its background algorithm (their §3.1) is four lines: take a coarse subsample of the pattern, then repeatedly replace each sample by the mean of its two neighbours wherever it stands more than c above that mean,

mi = (pi+1 + pi−1)/2,    pi ← mi   if pi > mi + c (A.1)

and interpolate the eroded samples back onto the measured grid. A peak is a local maximum and is pulled down pass by pass; a background is not. Their own settings are every twentieth point of a 0.01° film scan, c ≈ 0.02 on the eight-bit scale of their microdensitometer, and about thirty passes.

It is a background component, not an estimator the other components are fitted to. The eroded curve is the background — nothing is fitted to it and there is no degree to choose — which is how HighScore presents it and how ClayQuant offers it, in the same list as the polynomials. Its two parameters carry HighScore's names and defaults so that a setting means the same thing in both:
ParameterPaperHighScoreHere
Granularityevery twentieth pointnumber of intervals, slider 0–50, 15–30 recommended, literature value 200–50, proposed from the scan
Bending factorc = 0.02 of 255slider, 0–100 0–100, proposed at 0
Passesabout 30not exposed30

Granularity is counted in points, as both the paper and HighScore count it, and bending 1 is anchored on the paper's own c, so that 0 is their strictly-linear first form. That anchoring is a choice rather than a conversion: HighScore's slider position is not documented as a multiple of anything, so the same number in both need not give exactly the same curve. Given what the bending factor is measured to do below — almost nothing — that matters less than it sounds. The passes are left at the paper's thirty and not exposed, for the same reason HighScore does not expose them: with the passes fixed, granularity is the single control of how wide a feature is removed.

Does it do what the paper says

Three properties are claimed or implied, and all three hold exactly rather than approximately:

PropertyTestResult
A straight background survives (their Fig. 1a) a line of slope −30 counts/°2 × 10−13 counts
A convex background survivesa/x1.5, the shape of the direct-beam tail0 counts
A curved background survives up to a stated limit a parabola at 1.1 and at 0.5 times the predicted bound kept / eroded

The convex case is the one that matters here, and it holds for the same reason it holds for SNIP (§A.11): where the background is convex, the mean of two neighbours is never below the point itself, so (A.1) cannot fire. The direct-beam tail of an oriented mount is returned untouched by both estimators, which is the property the whole low-angle analysis rests on.

The third row needs a statement the paper does not make. At the fixed point of (A.1) the second difference of the retained background is exactly −2c, so with a sample spacing h

d2p/dx2 ≥ −2c/h2 (A.2)

— c is neither a tolerance nor a smoothing parameter but precisely the largest downward curvature a background is allowed to keep. Two things follow: c scales with the intensity, so it is taken here as a fraction of the range of the sampled data rather than in counts, and it scales with h2, so changing the sampling changes c. (A.2) is verified by switching the retention of a parabola across the predicted bound.

Two things the paper's own description gets wrong for modern data

The reach is diffusive, not linear. Replacing a point by the mean of its neighbours is one explicit step of the diffusion equation, so the passes do not march outwards one sample each. Measured on Gaussian peaks, the width at which half the height is removed is

FWHM = 2.2 · h · √n (A.3)

for n passes, where h is granularity × step. It holds to 2 % from 5 to 120 passes and over a fourfold range of h. The consequences are the practical content of the granularity slider. The paper's twenty points on a 0.01° film scan, at thirty passes, reach about 2.4° — not the 12° a linear reading of the iteration gives, and well matched to the sharp lines of a Guinier camera. The same granularity on this laboratory's 0.0167° step reaches 4.0°, because granularity is counted in points and the points are further apart; that is, as it happens, the stripping width ClayQuant had already settled on independently (§6). Since the number that matters is the one in degrees and the slider is in points, the interface reports the conversion beneath the slider. Unlike SNIP's window the cutoff is soft: a feature of exactly the stated width keeps half its height.

Granularity510 203040
Spacing on a 0.0167° scan0.084°0.167° 0.334°0.501°0.668°
Width half-removed, 30 passes1.0°2.0° 4.0°6.0°8.1°

The bending factor is weak at the bottom of its range, not inert — a correction. An earlier version of this section reported it as inert to 0.03 % of the intensity range, on the strength of a slider running 0 to 4. The range was the error: HighScore's own runs to 100, and over that span the parameter moves a baseline by 2.3 to 12.4 % of the intensity range on real patterns. The first few units really do almost nothing — 0.08 to 0.16 % from 0 to 1, about 0.4 % by 4 — which is why a slider stopping at 4 made it look like a control that did not work, and why it now runs the full distance.

Bending factor1410 2550100
Baseline moved, glycol mount0.16 %0.35 % 1.4 %3.7 %4.3 %5.4 %
Baseline moved, hectorite0.09 %0.52 % 1.3 %2.4 %4.7 %12.4 %
Rwp penalty, worst of 8 mounts0.5 1.54.27.89.3 11.9

Against bending 0, as a percentage of the intensity range; the last row in points of Rwp.

Granularity from 10 to 40 still moves the baseline by 30 %, so it remains the parameter to set first. And which bending value to prefer is settled rather than open: over eight glycol mounts, Rwp is lowest at 0 on every one and rises monotonically to 4.6–11.9 points worse at 100. The reason is (A.2) — a real clay background's downward curvature far exceeds the bound, so raising the allowance cannot help the baseline follow the background; all it does is let the baseline sit higher and take more of the broad basal intensity out. The slider reaches 100 because HighScore's does and because a control should be able to show what it does, not because the upper end is a good place to work.

One implementation question the paper leaves open answers itself. Their loop is in place, so a sample already lowered in this pass is what its right-hand neighbour sees, which makes a pass asymmetric in the direction of travel. Forming every mean from the previous pass instead gives a different answer while the erosion is still relaxing — 2.8 % of the intensity range after one pass — and an identical one from about 21 passes, where the relaxation reaches its fixed point. At the paper's thirty and above the choice does not matter, so the paper's own order is kept.

Against the stripping, on real patterns

Both estimators were asked for the same thing — remove everything narrower than 4°, keep the rest — on all 39 real patterns available. The disagreement is one-sided for practical purposes: over the whole set Sonneveld–Visser lies between 0.18 % of the intensity range below the stripped estimate and 36 % above it. Where it lies depends on the specimen, and systematically:

MountRange, counts Largest difference% of range
Prochlorite517501820.35

Sonneveld–Visser minus peak-stripped, both at a 4° width. Median over the twelve single-phase mounts, 5.2 %.

The ordering is not random. The well-crystallised mounts — prochlorite, kaolinite, chlorite, both corundums — agree to under 2 %, because a pattern of sharp peaks on a smooth background is what both estimators were designed for and there is nothing to disagree about. The disagreement is concentrated in the diffuse specimens: the synthetic hectorite that is close to X-ray amorphous, the bentonite carrying opal-CT, the laponite, the smectites. There the two estimators are deciding whether a broad hump is background or signal, and they decide differently. Of the 11.6 % on hectorite, running the erosion on the logarithm rather than on the counts accounts for about a third and the softness of the cutoff for the rest.

What it changes in the answer

That difference does not stay in the background. Eight glycol-solvated mounts were fitted twice, identically except for the estimator:

Mount123 4567 8
Rwp, peak-stripped42.3 44.546.5 47.250.0 72.377.3 78.6
Rwp, Sonneveld–Visser49.8 47.651.050.956.9 85.583.984.7

Per cent. Same library, same model, same 4° width, same fitting range.

The stripping fits better on all eight, by 2 to 13 points. And the phase percentages move with it: the largest change to any one phase's weight percent is a median of 20 percentage points and reaches 38 — on an illite/smectite, a kaolinite or a chlorite/smectite depending on the mount. A change of that size from a choice invisible in the reported table is the finding of this section.

The fair objection is that 4° may simply suit one estimator and not the other, so the width was swept for both:

Width1°2° 3°4°6° 8°12°
Mount 1, Sonneveld–Visser53.053.8 51.849.849.649.6 49.6
Mount 1, peak-stripped51.843.4 42.642.3 42.442.5 42.5
Mount 4, Sonneveld–Visser64.357.0 53.250.949.749.7 49.7
Mount 4, peak-stripped53.948.6 47.847.246.8 46.746.7

Rwp in per cent. At its own best width Sonneveld–Visser still loses on every mount tried, by 2 to 7 points, so the result is not an artefact of the setting. It also saturates above about 6°, which (A.1) explains: the erosion reaches a fixed point beyond which more passes change nothing, so unlike the stripping it has a floor it cannot go below.

Reading the two parameters off the measurement

Neither parameter has a value that is right in general, and the interface therefore proposes both from the glycol-solvated scan when the patterns are loaded — that mount, because it is the one the quantification is made on (§2.1) and the one whose broad interstratified intensity a background most easily eats. The two are settled differently, because only one of them is determined by the data.

Granularity follows from what has to survive. The erosion removes a feature from the baseline once its reach exceeds the feature's width, so the reach has to clear the broadest reflection meant to stay in the signal. That width is measured rather than assumed, and measured with the paper's own remaining two sections: the pattern is stripped generously, the noise of what is left is σnoise from their §3.2, the stretches standing above μ+3σ are their §3.3 peak groups, and the broadest of those is the width to clear — by a factor of two, which comes from (A.3) rather than from taste: at a reach equal to a feature's width half its height is left in the baseline, and at twice the width a few per cent. Two limits are imposed on the answer. It is never below the 4° that eleven mounts supported for the stripping, because a scan in which no broad reflection rises above the noise is not evidence that none is present, and erring upwards leaves background in the signal rather than taking signal out. And it is never above a quarter of the scan, past which the background would be defined by a handful of samples; where that cap binds, the suggestion says so, because a feature that wide cannot be told from background by any local test and the judgement is the analyst's.

Bending was measured, not chosen. Asking the fit which value it prefers is the wrong question for granularity and the right one here. Asked over eight glycol mounts at eight granularities, and again across the whole 0–100 range, Rwp was lowest at bending 0 on every mount, and worse by up to 11.9 points at 100. The reason is (A.2): a real clay background's downward curvature exceeds the bound any bending factor in HighScore's range can grant, so the allowance cannot do the job the paper introduced it for, and all that is left of it is a baseline sitting slightly higher — which on an oriented mount means slightly more of the broad basal intensity taken out as background. So 0 is proposed. This disagrees with the paper's own advice, and deliberately: they introduced c because a film background on a 0–255 scale really was gently curved enough for the bound to bite, which a clay diffractogram is not.

Granularity is deliberately not chosen by fit quality, though it would have been easy to. Swept against a real fit, Rwp falls almost monotonically as granularity rises — on four of the eight mounts the best value was the largest tried — because a lower baseline always lets the fit explain more of the pattern whether or not what was removed was background. It is the same bias that makes the residual of a whole-pattern fit useless as a measure of missing material (§2.13), and a pre-screen built on it would have recommended taking out as much as possible.

What it gives on real data. Over eleven measured patterns the proposal is granularity 20–22 and bending 0, so on these mounts it mostly confirms the default rather than changing it — which is itself worth having, since it says the default is right for this specimen rather than in general. It separates the two mounts carrying a genuinely broad 2.07° feature, where the measurement rather than the floor decides, from the nine where it does not. On synthetic patterns it tracks a planted reflection from 0.2° to 8°, and reports the cap beyond that.

Planted reflection0.2°2° 4°8°12°
Width measured0.20°2.00° 3.96°9.27°not found
Granularity proposed2020 394320
Decided byfloorfloormeasurementcap floor

A 12° feature is a third of a 37° scan, and no local test distinguishes it from background; the pre-screen does not find it and falls back to the floor, which is the safe direction but is a limit worth knowing.

A defect in the noise level had to be fixed before any of this worked, and it is the paper's own algorithm that carries it. Their §3.2 takes σ over everything, peaks included, then rejects above μ+3σ and repeats until σ settles. On a film scan of sharp lines the contamination is small and the loop tightens. On a pattern carrying a broad feature the feature is a fifth of the points, σ comes out inflated by two orders of magnitude, μ+3σ lands above every point in the pattern, and the first pass rejects nothing — whereupon σ not moving satisfies their stopping rule. Measured on an 8° Gaussian standing on noise of 18 counts, the returned level was 2900, with a threshold above the feature's own height, so the feature was reported as noise and could not set a granularity. Seeding the loop from the median and the median absolute deviation instead, which a fifth of the points does not move, returns 24 and finds the feature. The residual third of overestimate is left as it is: a threshold slightly too high is slightly less sensitive, which is the safe direction here.

The noise level that goes with it

Their §3.2 is implemented too, because a background estimate is only half of what the paper's workflow produces: the other half is the level against which a feature of the difference signal counts as real. Take the background-subtracted data, compute its mean and standard deviation, reject everything above μ + 3σ, and repeat until σ settles; what is left is noise, and the paper takes its full range to be 6σ.

The one thing to get right is that the clipping is one-sided, and the paper's step (4) says so explicitly. The contaminating population is the peaks, which lie above the background and nowhere below it, so rejecting symmetrically at |i − μ| > 3σ discards the lower half of the very noise being measured and returns a σ too small. Tested against normal noise of known width contaminated with peaks two hundred times its height, the plain standard deviation is more than ten times too large and the clipped estimate recovers the true value to 10 %. The paper's N ≈ 500 points was a concession to a 1975 computer; all the data is used by default and agrees with a 500-point subsample to 12 %.

Conclusion, and what the second estimator is for

The method is implemented faithfully, passes every property its paper claims for it, and is offered in the interface and on the command line. Peak stripping remains the default, for a measured reason rather than a preference: Sonneveld–Visser puts the baseline higher, and on an oriented clay mount what lies immediately above the baseline is the broad basal intensity of the interstratified phases — the signal being quantified. Taking it out as background is the error §5.4 warns about, arrived at by a different route. It is also the reason the disagreement is largest exactly on the expandable clays, which are the phases the analysis is least able to check by other means.

What the second estimator is genuinely for is the question that prompted it. The difference between two independent estimators, on the same pattern at the same width, is a direct measure of how much of the background is a matter of method. On a well-crystallised mount that measure is under 2 % of the intensity range and the background can be treated as determined. On a diffuse one it is a tenth of the range, and no amount of care with the model will make it better, because the disagreement is about what the background is and not about how to fit it. Any specimen where the two estimators disagree by more than a few per cent is a specimen whose reported percentages carry that disagreement, and running both is now the cheapest way to find out.

Appendix D — Provenance of the accompanying-mineral structures

The 209 structures below are those of the TOPAS structure library used during development. They are not distributed with ClayQuant and are not part of it: the library is user-supplied, imported by clayquant-import-structures (§4.3), and every ClayQuant installation may use a different one. The table is given so that any pattern the program calculates can be traced to the structure it came from, and that structure to its source database and entry.

Why the citations are not printed here. Of the 209 entries, 200 are ICSD, 3 AMCSD and 2 COD, and 4 carry no identifier. ICSD is a licensed database with no open lookup from an entry number to its publication, so those citations could not be retrieved and verified for this manual, and they have deliberately not been guessed: an invented reference is worse than an absent one. The identifiers below are exact, taken from the library file itself, and each resolves to its full bibliographic record in the database named — through an ICSD subscription, through rruff.geo.arizona.edu/AMS for AMCSD, or through crystallography.net for COD, all of which report the original publication for the entry. A machine-readable copy with an empty citation column to fill in is in the repository as docs/structure_provenance.csv.

The four clay mineral structures are not in this table: they are integral to the program, are named in §4.2, and their publications are cited in full in §10.

PANalytical XRDML.xrdml Intensities from <counts> or <intensities>; multiple appended scans are concatenated; positions from a start/end range or an explicit list. Wavelengths, goniometer radius, divergence slit, counting time and sample identifier are read as metadata.
Two-column text.xy, .txt, .dat, .asc 2θ and intensity. Comment and header lines are skipped; comma, tab and space separation are accepted.
Bruker RAW.raw Binary; the common RAW1.01 and RAW4 variants. Support is best-effort — if a file is not read, export it as two-column text from the vendor software.
CIF.cif The subset produced by ICSD, COD and AMCSD exports: cell, an explicit symmetry-operation loop, and an atom-site loop with occupancies and Biso or Uiso.
TOPAS structure library.xml jEdit macro-menu form; str blocks with cell, space group and site lines.
Pattern library.npz Compressed NumPy archive holding the grid, the pattern matrix, and per-entry and library metadata.
